channel.title: The Empirical Dad
channel.description: Evidence-based parenting for dads who don't plan to slow down. A daily briefing from the first positive test to age three, numbered by the day of pregnancy the way your OB counts it. Every claim is graded out loud as established, strong or emerging, and every risk gets a real number. One angle a day (body, brain, physiology, parents, adventure, protocol, myths) and one small action at the end. A personal research briefing, not medical advice.

item.title: Day 87 · Week 12 — Parents: the two of you
item.description:
The small average drop and the sudden step at the birth, the childless couples who drift too, what a husband's fondness predicts, and the eight-class programme that changed the outcome in two trials.
What a first baby does to a couple, measured. Twenge 2003 (97 articles, 47,692 people): parents slightly less satisfied than non-parents (d = −0.19), largest for mothers of infants (38% vs 62% highly satisfied), explained by role conflict and restricted freedom. Mitnick 2009 (37 longitudinal studies): small declines to 11 months, moderate by 12–14 months — but childless newlyweds decline similarly. Lawrence 2008 (156 couples with childless controls): parenthood hastens decline; planning and pre-pregnancy satisfaction protect. Doss 2009 (218 couples, 8 years): a sudden, persistent, small-to-medium drop at the birth in mothers and fathers alike, against a gradual slope in non-parents. Shapiro, Gottman & Carrère 2000: a husband's fondness and awareness predicted mothers' satisfaction holding steady; negativity, disappointment and chaos predicted decline. The trials: the Cowans' couples groups (less decline over 66 months), and Family Foundations — coparenting classes before and after the birth — in 169 couples (coparental support, maternal depression and anxiety, infant regulation; effects to 3.5 years) and 399 couples (better on two-thirds of measures, large effects on family violence, most benefit for higher-risk couples). Pinquart & Teubert's 142-trial meta-analysis as the reality check (couple adjustment d = 0.13).
Today's action: Tonight, ask your partner one question and only listen: 'What are you most worried will change between us after the baby comes?' No solving, no defending — a follow-up question or two. Then start a section called 'Us' in the pregnancy file and write one line with what she said.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 86 · Week 12 — Physiology: her immune system runs on a clock
item.description:
The three phases, the cells your baby leaves in her for decades, the flu numbers by trimester, the two-day antiviral window, and the conditions that go quiet and then rebound.
Pregnancy is not immune suppression. Medawar's 1953 puzzle (a half-foreign fetus that is never rejected) and the modern answer: a modulated, timed programme in three phases — inflammatory implantation and first trimester, anti-inflammatory second trimester, inflammatory labour (Mor & Cardenas 2010). The Stanford immune clock (Aghaeepour 2017): mass cytometry on 18 women's blood read the stage of pregnancy and validated in 10 more. Fetal microchimerism: male cells in 6 of 8 mothers of sons, up to 27 years later (Bianchi 1996). Which infections are worse — influenza, hepatitis E, herpes simplex, malaria; more susceptibility to listeria — and which are not (Kourtis 2014). Flu by trimester in Tennessee Medicaid (odds up to 4.67 at term; 10.5 flu-attributable events per 10,000 women-months in the third trimester), the 2009 pandemic (1% of the population, 5% of deaths; ICU 56.9% if antivirals began after four days vs 9.4% within two), COVID (fewer symptoms but ICU OR 2.13), and the Bangladesh trial (63% fewer lab-confirmed infant flu cases after maternal vaccination). Multiple sclerosis relapses down about 70% in the third trimester and up after birth (PRIMS); rheumatoid arthritis improving in about half with active disease, 39% postpartum flare (PARA). The father as the household's main route of infection, and the same-day call.
Today's action: If you haven't had this season's flu vaccine, book it this week, and check that hers is on the list for her next appointment. In the pregnancy file, next to the practice's numbers, add: 'Flu symptoms or fever: call the same day. Antivirals work best within two days. Don't wait for a test.'
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 85 · Week 12 — Brain: the first preference
item.description:
The right arm at ten weeks, the thumb at fifteen, sixty of sixty, the spinal cord that picks a side before the brain, the one in ten, and the left-handers who didn't die young.
The Brain episode on handedness, which starts long before the first crayon. At 10 weeks 85% of 72 fetuses moved the right arm more than the left, at an age when the brain probably isn't driving the arms (Hepper 1998). From 15 weeks most fetuses suck the right thumb, independent of position (Hepper 1991), and in the one follow-up, 60 of 60 right-thumb-suckers were right-handed at 10–12 years and 10 of 15 left-thumb-suckers were left-handed (Hepper 2005). The preference may begin in the spinal cord, with epigenetically regulated left–right gene expression (Ocklenburg 2017, five fetuses). Left-handedness prevalence is 9.3–18.1% depending on definition, best estimate 10.6%, with cultural pressure lowering observed rates (Papadatou-Pastou 2020); genes explain ~25% of variation and the shared family environment none (Medland 2006, 21,127 twin pairs); 41 loci for left-handedness and 7 for ambidexterity in 1.77 million people (Cuellar-Partida 2021); blood methylation captures little (Odintsova 2022). The old claim that left-handers die younger was an artefact of switched children (Salive 1993). Verdict: nothing to optimise; let the hand choose.
Today's action: In the pregnancy file's 'First weeks' section, add one line: 'Hand: let them choose. Don't move the crayon.' At the next scan, watch the arms — the preference is already there.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 84 · Week 12 — Body: the reflex kit
item.description:
The startle, the grasp, the suck and the swallow, the gut that comes home from the cord, the fifty-six percent sex call, and the three feeding cues you'll read at four in the morning.
Week 12 opens, the last full week of the first trimester. Your baby is about 5.4 cm head to bottom (NHS), skeleton hardening, placenta likely feeding them. The Body episode is the reflexes: what a reflex is and why a baby with almost no cortex can run one (spinal and brainstem circuits; MedlinePlus); the startle, seen from ~8 weeks and one of the movements that rises then falls (de Vries, Visser & Prechtl), becoming the newborn Moro reflex with its brainstem centre and diagnostic weight (Futagi 2012); the palmar and plantar grasp and the AAP timetable for when each newborn reflex fades; sucking and swallowing, the fetus as a heavy drinker for its size (Ross & Nijland 1997) and why no ultrasound can measure how much; the gut returning from the umbilical cord (still visible in 5% at 12 weeks; Bogers 2019); why a first-trimester sex call is at best 56% right (Bogers 2018); and why suck–swallow–breathe coordination is one of the last skills to mature (Lau 2016), with the three AAP feeding cues — rooting, sucking, hand to mouth.
Today's action: Open the pregnancy file and add a section called 'First weeks' with two lines: 'Feeding cues: rooting, sucking, hand to mouth. Feed before the crying.' and 'Reflexes fade: stepping and startle by about two to four months, rooting by four, palm grip by six, fencing by seven, foot grip by twelve.'
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.itunes:title: Day 84 · Week 12 — Body: the reflex kit

item.title: Day 83 · Week 11 — Myths: she has to sleep on her left side from now on, pelvic floor training makes the birth harder, and sit-ups split her…
item.description:
Three myths about the months ahead. Sleep: the vena cava compression is real in late pregnancy, and from 28 weeks going to sleep on the back was linked to 2.6 times the odds of late stillbirth (Cronin 2019 IPD meta-analysis, 851 cases, 2,257 controls) on a baseline of roughly 1–9 per 1,000 — but the right side is as safe as the left (aOR 1.04), and before 28–30 weeks a prospective cohort of 8,706 first pregnancies (nuMoM2b) found no link between back or right-side sleep and stillbirth, growth restriction or hypertensive disorders. Pelvic floor training: in 18,865 Norwegian first-time mothers, training three or more times a week did not increase severe tears, episiotomy, instrumental birth or emergency caesarean, and a meta-analysis of 12 trials found slightly shorter labour stages with no change in tears. Abdominal separation: present in 100% of first-time mothers at 35 weeks and 33% at 21 weeks, narrowing over the first year, not linked to back or pelvic pain; antenatal exercise associated with 35% less diastasis on weak evidence; curl-ups narrow rather than widen the gap. Why ACOG's advice on avoiding long periods supine during exercise is about blood flow, not abdominal muscles.
Today's action: In the shared calendar, put one entry at 28 weeks (Day 196): 'Side-sleeping from tonight, either side. Pillows.' In the pregnancy file's Pelvic floor section, add: 'Every squeeze ends with a full let-go.' Tonight, tell her the short version: any sleep position she likes, for now.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 82 · Week 11 — Protocol: the pelvic floor, week one
item.description:
Forty-six trials, the one woman in three who leaks after birth, the half who squeeze the wrong way, and the first seven days.
The pelvic floor training block begins. What the pelvic floor is (the levator ani sling that holds the bladder and bowel closed and the organs up) and what pregnancy and birth ask of it — in an MRI-based model the medial pubococcygeus stretches to 3.26 times its resting length. How common leaking is: 41% of pregnant women (44 studies, 88,305 women) and 31% in the year after birth, with prevalence at one year back near third-trimester levels. The 2020 Cochrane review (46 trials, 10,832 women): early, structured training in continent women cut incontinence in late pregnancy by 62% and at 3–6 months postpartum by 29% (high-quality evidence), with smaller effects in population programmes, no proven benefit for women already leaking, and almost no harms. The Trondheim trial (301 first-time mothers): 32% vs 48% leaking at 36 weeks, 20% vs 32% at three months — one in six prevented. Bump 1991: after verbal instruction only 49% contract correctly and 25% bear down. NICE NG210 and NG123: encourage for all, supervise for higher risk or existing leaks, at least 8 contractions three times a day, keep it up for life. How to find the muscles, the week-one plan, the knack, the warning signs and the father's part.
Today's action: Tonight, set three daily reminders on her phone (and yours if you join in) tied to breakfast, lunch and brushing teeth, labelled 'squeeze, lift, let go'. Add a 'Pelvic floor' section to the pregnancy file with two lines: any leaking now, or a mother or sister with incontinence or prolapse (yes/no); and the question for the next visit — a referral to a pelvic health physiotherapist to check technique. First set tonight: five slow squeezes, lying down.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 81 · Week 11 — Adventure: water
item.description:
What immersion does to a pregnant body, seventy-four thousand Danish swimmers, the cold plunge with four studies behind it, the surf break after twelve weeks, and the tank that stays on the boat.
Water, the friendliest environment of the pregnancy. Your baby, about 4.5–5 cm, already lives afloat at body temperature. Immersion physiology (Katz 1996): hydrostatic pressure shifts tissue fluid back into the circulation (less swelling, a diuresis), buoyancy takes the load off loosening joints and removes most fall risk, and water draws heat away about 25 times faster than air — heart rate, blood pressure and fetal heart-rate changes are lower during water exercise than on land. ACOG Committee Opinion 804 lists swimming and water aerobics as safe to start or continue. The chlorine question: in the Danish National Birth Cohort (74,486 pregnancies), swimming showed no harm, with preterm birth HR 0.80 and malformations OR 0.89 versus non-exercisers and results matching cyclists (Juhl 2010). Hot tubs and hot springs reverse the logic (Day 48). Open water: currents, company, turning back early, water quality after heavy rain, and ultraviolet reflection (Day 79). Cold water: the cold shock response and its habituation after about four immersions (Barwood 2024 meta-analysis); a 2025 consensus scoping review found only four studies on cold-water swimming in pregnancy, so not the time to start, and habituated swimmers go shorter, enter slowly and never alone (Shawe 2025). Surfing and water skiing are on ACOG's avoid list for falls; the pelvis protects the uterus until about 12–14 weeks; the board, the prone paddle and the abruption risk of blunt trauma. Scuba is a clear no: no lung filter for bubbles in the fetal circulation, and field data from 129 women and 1,465 dives too sparse to show safety (St Leger Dowse 2006; Reid & Lorenzo 2018). Snorkelling is fine.
Today's action: Add three lines to the pregnancy file: 'Swimming: yes, pool and open water with company.' 'Cold water: only if already habituated — short, slow entry, never alone; check with the OB if blood pressure is up.' 'No scuba until after the birth; snorkel instead.' Then look up the nearest pool's lap-swim times and put one swim in the calendar this week.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 80 · Week 11 — Parents: her mood
item.description:
The depression that peaks before the birth, the one in four who is anxious, the ten questions on the clipboard, and what a partner can see that a form can't.
Depression and anxiety during pregnancy, not after it. Your baby is about 4.5 cm and under 10 g, kidneys making urine and the placenta finishing its hormone handover. The numbers: depression in 7.4% of women in the first trimester and about 12–13% in the second and third (Bennett 2004, 21 studies, 19,284 women); in ALSPAC 13.5% were above the depression threshold at 32 weeks of pregnancy versus 9.1% at 8 weeks postpartum (Evans 2001); anxiety symptoms in 18.2%, 19.1% and 24.6% by trimester and an anxiety disorder in 15.2% (Dennis 2017, 102 studies, 221,974 women); antenatal anxiety roughly tripling the odds of postnatal depression (Heron 2004, 8,323 women). The risk factors that survive adjustment — life stress, low social support and domestic violence (Lancaster 2010). Why it matters: preterm birth RR 1.39 and low birth weight RR 1.49 where depression is categorised, with the confounding caveat (Grote 2010), and mental health conditions as the leading underlying cause of US pregnancy-related deaths (about 23%, CDC MMRC 2017–2019). The screening: ACOG CPG 4 (2023) — screen at the first visit, later in pregnancy and postpartum; the 10-item Edinburgh scale and its accuracy (sensitivity 81%, specificity 88% at ≥11; Levis 2020, 15,557 women); the Whooley questions and the 'would you like help?' question (specificity 94%, Arroll 2005). Treatment: counselling cuts onset by 39% in women at risk (USPSTF 2019, grade B); SSRIs and heart defects — RR 1.06 once depression is accounted for (Huybrechts 2014, 949,504 pregnancies). The partner's part: support and conflict in the Pilkington meta-analysis, the 29-woman Misri trial, the signs worth noticing over two weeks, how to raise it, and the situations that mean calling the same day — with the 988 Lifeline and the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline.
Today's action: Add a 'Mood' section to the pregnancy file with two lines: any history of depression or anxiety in either of you, and what helped; and the two numbers — 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) and the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline, 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262). Save the hotline in your phone.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 79 · Week 11 — Physiology: her skin
item.description:
The dark line, the mask and the sunscreen trial, what altitude and snow add, six trials of stretch-mark creams, and the itch without a rash that changes the birth plan.
Why pregnancy changes the skin: placental oestrogen, progesterone and melanocyte-stimulating signals, a larger blood volume, and rapid stretch. Pigment changes are near-universal (93% in a 2026 cross-sectional study): linea nigra, darker areolae, darkening moles (a markedly changing mole still needs checking) and melasma, which needs ultraviolet light — in one Moroccan study daily SPF 50+ broad-spectrum sunscreen cut new cases to 2.7% against a historical 53% (Lakhdar 2007, historical control). WHO: UV rises ~10% per 1,000 m and fresh snow reflects up to 80%. Palmar erythema and spider angiomas are oestrogen effects. Stretch marks affected 52% of 309 first-time mothers, more often younger women and those with higher BMI, more weight gain or a heavier baby (Atwal 2006); across six trials and 800 women no topical preparation clearly prevented them (Cochrane, RR 0.74, 0.53–1.03). Postpartum shedding at 2–4 months is normal. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — itch on palms and soles, no rash, worse at night — affects ~0.7% in the UK; stillbirth risk tracks peak bile acids: 0.13% below 40 µmol/L, 0.28% at 40–99, 3.44% at ≥100 (Ovadia 2019, IPD 5,269 women), which sets the timing of birth; ursodeoxycholic acid did not reduce adverse outcomes (PITCHES, 605 women).
Today's action: Add under the red flags in the pregnancy file: "Itching on palms or soles, no rash, worse at night: call the practice that week and ask for bile acids and liver function tests." Put a broad-spectrum SPF 50 sunscreen in the travel bag and a second by the front door.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.itunes:title: Day 79 · Week 11 — Physiology: her skin

item.title: Day 78 · Week 11 — Brain: touch, the first sense
item.description:
The mouth at seven and a half weeks, the palms this week, reflexes that bypass the brain, the waiting room under the cortex, and the father's chest.
Touch is the first sense to work. Humphrey's Pittsburgh films (Prog Brain Res 1964) traced the order: a hair stroked around the mouth draws a whole-body turn at about 7.5 weeks (~Day 52), the palms respond with a partial grasp at ~10.5–11 weeks (this week), the soles at ~12 and most of the body by ~14 — reflex arcs through the spinal cord and brainstem, not experience. The thalamic fibres that carry touch to the cortex wait for weeks in the transient subplate (Kostović & Judaš, 500+ brains) and connect in the late second and third trimester; the JAMA systematic review (Lee 2005) puts conscious pain perception unlikely before the third trimester, with the dissent (Derbyshire & Bockmann 2020) labelled as contested. Ordinary touch tunes the developing spinal circuits (Fitzgerald 2005). Third-trimester fetuses respond to a mother's touch on the abdomen in small 4D studies (Marx & Nagy 2015, 2017). After birth, C-tactile fibres code slow, pleasant stroking at 1–10 cm/s (Löken 2009); skin-to-skin contact across 46 trials raises breastfeeding at 1–4 months (RR 1.24), and a small trial found babies on the father's chest after caesarean cried less (Erlandsson 2007).
Today's action: Add a Birth plan section to the pregnancy file with one line: "If she can't do skin-to-skin straight away, I do it. Ask the hospital: can the father do skin-to-skin in theatre or recovery after a caesarean?"
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 77 · Week 11 — Body: the scan window opens
item.description:
A fetus the size of a fig, why the look waits until now, the fluid behind the neck, and what a hundred thousand first-trimester scans could and couldn't find.
Week eleven, and the 11–14-week scan window (ISUOG 2023: 11+0 to 14+0 weeks; FMF: crown-rump length 45–84 mm) opens today and closes on Day 98. Your baby is about 41 mm, the size of a fig, with four heart chambers, a visible stomach and bladder, and the gut back inside the abdomen. Why the window is set by the body: physiological gut herniation has resolved (so exomphalos can be diagnosed), the skull is mineralizing (so acrania can be seen), the neck fluid is measurable, and the fetus is big enough. What nuchal translucency is and the hypotheses for it (lymphatic, cardiac, connective tissue). With normal chromosomes, the chance of a baby alive and well falls from ~93% at the 95th–99th centile to ~15% at ≥6.5 mm (Souka 2005); heart defects rise from 0.8 to ~63 per 1,000 as NT thickens (Hyett 1999, 29,154 fetuses). The nasal bone as a soft marker (Cicero 2001: absent in 73% of trisomy 21 vs 0.5%). The first-trimester anatomy check: in 100,997 pregnancies, 1.7% had a structural anomaly and 27.6% of these were found at 11–13 weeks — some always (acrania, holoprosencephaly, abdominal-wall defects), some rarely (VSDs, cleft lip, late brain findings) (Syngelaki 2019); 46% of major anomalies in low-risk populations, higher with a checklist (Karim 2017). What happens after a finding, and the three questions to ask at the scan.
Today's action: Check that the 11–14-week scan is booked for a date between today and Day 97; if not, call the practice tomorrow. Write three questions on the scans page of the pregnancy file: Was the full anatomy check done? What was the NT and is it normal for the crown-rump length? Is there anything to recheck, and when?
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 76 · Week 10 — Myths: bed rest protects a pregnancy, rest prevents preterm birth, and a woman who wasn't a runner shouldn't start moving now
item.description:
The Myths episode on rest. Bed rest became standard obstetric treatment on intuition, not trials. For bleeding in the first half of pregnancy, the only Cochrane evidence is two trials with 84 women and no benefit (RR 1.54, 0.92–2.58); ACOG says not to recommend it, because most early losses are chromosomal and set at conception, and exercise does not raise miscarriage risk (Davenport 2019, OR 0.88). For preterm birth, the one qualifying Cochrane trial (1,266 women) found no difference (RR 0.92); six twin trials (636 women) found no reduction in birth before 34 weeks; and in 646 women with a short cervix, the 39% placed on activity restriction delivered preterm in 37% vs 17% (aOR 2.37) — no benefit. The costs: one hospital series found blood clots in 15.6 per 1,000 women on bed rest vs 0.8 per 1,000 others; bone loss, muscle wasting, weight loss, depression and lost income. Then the beginner myth: ACOG, WHO and Canada say inactive women should start and build gradually; a 765-woman Madrid RCT starting at 9–11 weeks found non-exercisers had ~3× the odds of gestational hypertension. Where rest genuinely belongs (named contraindications, ordinary fatigue), the script for bleeding, and the one question to ask if bed rest is suggested.
Today's action: Write one line at the top of the pregnancy file: 'Bleeding: call the practice the same day; bed rest is not the plan unless they give a specific reason,' with the after-hours number underneath. If your partner is just starting to move, book a 15-minute walk together for tomorrow.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 75 · Week 10 — Protocol: the hundred-and-fifty-minute plan
item.description:
What the minutes do to diabetes, blood pressure and mood, the one woman in eight who gets there, the talk test, and a calendar built for two.
The Protocol episode for week 10 turns the 150-minute guideline into a week. What the dose buys: in randomized trials, exercise alone cut the odds of gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension and preeclampsia by about 40% each, with ~140 minutes of moderate activity a week needed for at least a 25% reduction (Davenport 2018, 106 studies, 273,182 women), and cut the odds of prenatal depression by two thirds in five trials, though not postpartum depression or anxiety. In overweight and obese women, aerobic exercise lowered preterm birth (RR 0.62; Magro-Malosso 2017). The dissent: an older Cochrane review (Han 2012, 5 trials) found no clear effect on gestational diabetes, dominated by a trial where only about half the exercise group exercised. Only ~13% of US pregnant women meet the guideline (Hesketh & Evenson 2016), and self-report overestimates moderate activity by about an hour a week. WHO 2020, ACOG 804 and the Canadian guideline agree on at least 150 minutes over at least three days with strength work, every minute counting. Intensity by talk test and Borg 12–14, strength rules, the sickness weeks, sitting, the postpartum continuation, the stop list, a template week for active and newly active women, and the couple rule: a shared calendar, three sessions together, both totals counted.
Today's action: Tonight, open a shared calendar and put in next week's 150 minutes: five 30-minute blocks, two marked strength, at times she chooses around her sickness, at least three marked together. Add your own 150 minutes to the same calendar. On Sunday, write both weekly totals on the back page of the pregnancy file.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.itunes:title: Day 75 · Week 10 — Protocol: the hundred-and-fifty-minute plan

item.title: Day 74 · Week 10 — Adventure: cycling, running and swimming
item.description:
The guidelines that flipped from caution to keep going, the ceiling at ninety percent, the ground under the bike, and the pool that runs cool.
The Adventure episode for week 10, for couples who train. How the advice moved from ACOG's 1985 heart-rate cap to ACOG Committee Opinion 804 and the 2019 Canadian guideline, which says all women without contraindications should be active and found no harms. The miscarriage question with its largest analysis (Davenport 2019: 46 studies, 266,778 women, OR 0.88 for miscarriage). Running: 1,293 parkrun women who kept running delivered half a day later on average with same-size babies (Kuhrt 2018). Vigorous exercise into the third trimester: no effect on birthweight or growth in 32,080 cohort women and 623 trial participants (Beetham 2019). The ceiling: brief, reversible fetal bradycardia above ~90% of maximum heart rate in Olympic athletes (Salvesen 2012) and in 6 of 60 athletes during very-hard running intervals, none on the bike (Dalhaug 2025). Cycling's risk is the ground, not the effort: why the first trimester is protected by the pelvis and why trails and fast group rides come off the list first. Swimming: no hazard from pool water in 74,486 Danish pregnancies (Juhl 2010), and water exercise up to 33.4 °C for 45 minutes keeps core temperature well below 39 °C (Ravanelli 2019). Heat perception in a 32 °C chamber (Smallcombe 2021), the ACOG stop list, and the father's job: train with her, own the logistics, know the stop list.
Today's action: This week, do one session with your partner at her pace — a run, ride or swim of her choosing — using the talk test as the only intensity rule. If it's a ride, pick a flat, familiar, low-traffic route and check both bikes first. Say the stop list out loud once before you set off.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 73 · Week 10 — Parents: your weight and your sleep
item.description:
The four pounds of fatherhood, the partner effect that triples the odds of change, the father's BMI in the child's, sixty-two minutes against thirteen, and the hours below which you don't drive.
The father's own body as a lever in the household. Garfield's 20-year Add Health cohort (10,253 young men): becoming a resident father was linked to a 2.6% BMI rise, about 4.4 lb for a six-foot man, while non-fathers lost about 1.4 lb. Jackson, Steptoe & Wardle (JAMA Intern Med 2015, 3,722 couples): when one partner changed, the other was about three times as likely to lose weight (men 26% vs 10%), five times as likely to become active (67% vs 26%) and twelve times as likely to quit smoking (48% vs 8%) — and a newly changed partner beat a always-healthy one. Fleten's MoBa study of 29,216 families: father's and mother's BMI predicted the child's at age three equally (0.13 vs 0.12 per SD), pointing to genes and the household over the womb. Healthy Dads, Healthy Kids trials (−7.6 kg vs 0 at 6 months; −3.3 vs +0.1 kg in the community trial) as the case for father-framed change. Then sleep: the AASM/SRS ≥7-hour consensus; short sleep and obesity (OR 1.55, Cappuccio 2008); Richter's German panel showing mothers lose 62 minutes a night after a birth against fathers' 13, with neither recovered at six years; 46% of pregnant women sleeping poorly (Sedov 2018); moderate–severe sleep apnoea in ~10% of men aged 30–49 (Peppard 2013); and Tefft's crash odds by hours slept (1.3 at 6 h, 1.9 at 5, 2.9 at 4, 15.1 under 4).
Today's action: Tonight, set a bedtime alarm seven and a half hours before your morning alarm and run it for seven nights, noting each morning how many hours you actually slept. Write the average on a page with your name at the back of the Day 61 pregnancy file; if it's under seven, change one thing. And ask your partner: 'Do I snore, and does it wake you?' — then believe the answer.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 72 · Week 10 — Physiology: the weight
item.description:
Where twelve kilograms actually go, the four ranges, the flat first trimester, the one woman in three who lands in range, and what a million pregnancies say about missing it.
Weight gain in pregnancy, built from the parts. Hytten's classic breakdown of a ~12.5 kg gain: baby 3.4 kg, placenta ~0.65, amniotic fluid ~0.8, uterus ~1, breasts ~0.4, extra blood ~1.25, tissue fluid ~1.7 and ~3.3 kg of fat laid down as a reserve for late pregnancy and breastfeeding — so the baby is only about a quarter of it. Why the first trimester should be nearly flat (0.5–2 kg total; mild loss with nausea is common, but >5% loss is an RCOG marker of hyperemesis). The IOM 2009 ranges adopted by ACOG and CDC (28–40, 25–35, 15–25 and 11–20 lb by pre-pregnancy BMI; about a pound a week from the second trimester at normal weight) and the calorie numbers that replace 'eating for two' (0, ~340, ~450 extra a day). Only about one US woman in three lands in range and nearly half gain more (CDC MMWR 2015). Goldstein's JAMA 2017 meta-analysis of 1.3 million pregnancies gives the risks both ways with absolute differences; the LifeCycle IPD meta-analysis (196,670 women) shows starting weight carries most of the risk and the gain range is a weak individual predictor; Nehring 2011 shows ~3 kg more retained at 3 years. Cochrane (49 trials, 11,444 women) and Teede 2022 (117 trials, 34,546 women): diet and activity programmes cut excessive gain by ~20% and gestational diabetes by ~20%. NICE's no-routine-reweighing approach versus US practice, and why the dad's job is the kitchen and the calendar, never the scale.
Today's action: Find the booking weight and height on the first-visit record (or ask your partner if she'd rather tell you), work out the BMI category, and write the category and its IOM range on the lab page of the Day 61 pregnancy file next to yesterday's two numbers. Then close the file — the scale is the clinic's job. Yours this week: cook one dinner she can actually eat, and offer a walk afterwards.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 71 · Week 10 — Brain: the metal in the wiring
item.description:
Iron for energy, myelin and dopamine, the blood count from the first visit, fifty-seven trials, and the half-million Swedish children.
Iron and the unfinished brain. The developing brain can use up to 60% of total metabolic rate, and iron runs three of its jobs — mitochondrial energy, myelination by oligodendrocytes, and dopamine synthesis — with the hippocampus especially exposed (Barks & Georgieff 2018). Most fetal iron moves in the third trimester, but reserves are set now; when iron is short the fetus favours red cells over brain, so anemia is a late sign. Prevalence: 18% of US pregnant women iron deficient, 29.7% in the third trimester (NHANES); >80% by the third trimester in an Irish cohort of 641. ACOG PB 233: CBC in the first trimester and at 24–28 weeks, anemia thresholds Hb <11/10.5/11 g/dL, ferritin <30 µg/L consistent with deficiency, low-dose iron for nearly all. Cochrane 2024 (57 trials, 48,971 women): iron-deficiency anemia at term 5.0% vs 18.4%, low birth weight 5.2% vs 6.1%, no child-brain outcome. Wiegersma 2019 (532,232 Swedish children): anemia diagnosed ≤30 weeks linked to intellectual disability (OR 2.20), autism (1.44) and ADHD (1.37); later anemia was not. The USPSTF 2024 'insufficient' statement and why it doesn't contradict ACOG; RDA 27 mg, UL 45 mg, nausea from iron, alternate-day dosing as emerging, food pairing with vitamin C, and why liver is off the menu.
Today's action: Open the patient portal and find the first-visit blood count. Write the haemoglobin and, if present, the ferritin on the lab page of the Day 61 pregnancy file. If haemoglobin is under 11 g/dL or no ferritin was measured, add to the Questions page: 'Was ferritin checked, and should she be on more than the prenatal's iron?' Check the iron line on the prenatal label, and note if the vitamin is worsening her nausea.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 70 · Week 10 — Body: embryo to fetus
item.description:
The organ inventory, the window that has mostly closed, the risk curve after a normal scan, and the sickness that peaks before it breaks.
The day the embryo becomes a fetus: day 56 after fertilization, the end of Carnegie stage 23, about 30 mm and a few grams, heart at ~180 bpm, milk-tooth buds in the jaw. What the change of name marks (organogenesis ends; growth and maturation begin — a roughly thousand-fold weight gain to term) and a system-by-system inventory: heart, limbs, face, gut and kidneys built in plan; palate and genitals finishing; lungs and brain present and far from done. The teratology windows (all-or-none, embryonic, fetal) and why the Day 54 medication rules still stand. Tong 2008: after a normal scan with a heartbeat in 696 asymptomatic women, later miscarriage risk fell from 9.4% at 6 weeks to 0.5–0.7% at 9–10 weeks, with age and bleeding changing the numbers. Lacroix 2000: nausea in 74%, morning-only in 1.8%, peaking at 11–13 weeks, resolved in half by 14 weeks and 90% by 22. Red flags for hyperemesis, and why the FDA advises against home Dopplers.
Today's action: Offer to keep a four-week sickness log on your phone so she doesn't have to: one line a day — nausea 0–10, number of vomits, fluids kept down yes/no. If it isn't easing by about 14 weeks (Day 98), or any red flag appears (no fluids kept down for a day, weight loss, dark or scant urine, dizziness on standing, blood in vomit), take the log to the practice.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.itunes:title: Day 70 · Week 10 — Body: embryo to fetus

item.title: Day 69 · Week 9 — Myths: boy or girl
item.description:
The heartbeat over a hundred and forty, the basketball bump, the lunar calendar tested on 2.8 million births, timing and cereal, the ring on a thread, and the one piece of folklore that is partly true.
The sex-prediction folklore, each myth against the study that tested it. Where your baby is: Carnegie stage 23, ~30 mm, the last day of the embryonic period, with SRY switching the gonads at 6–7 weeks post-fertilization and the external anatomy not yet readable. The sex ratio at conception is 0.5 (Orzack 2015), so every method is right half the time. Heart rate: no sex difference in 212 pregnancies across 2,261 visits (Genuis 1996) or in 477 first-trimester scans (girls 151.7 vs boys 154.9 bpm; McKenna 2006) — it tracks age, not sex. Bump shape and morning-sickness folklore failed in 104 women (Perry 1999), and maternal intuition was no better than chance (Genuis 1996). The Chinese lunar calendar on 2,840,755 Swedish births: kappa 0.0002 (Villamor 2010). Timing of intercourse made no difference (Wilcox 1995, NEJM). The breakfast-cereal finding (Mathews 2008) was most likely a multiple-testing false positive (Young 2009). The ring on a thread, urine chemistry (and the drain-cleaner hazard) and the six-week placenta method have no published validation. The partly true one: severe sickness is linked to girls (54.1% vs 48.7% overall; Mitsuda 2019; Askling 1999) — a real association and still a nearly useless predictor.
Today's action: For fun: tonight each of you writes a boy/girl guess and the method behind it (heartbeat, bump, dream, calendar, a real coin toss); add two grandparents' guesses and methods. Seal them in an envelope dated Day 69, put it in the back of the Day 61 pregnancy file, and open it the day you find out.

item.content:encoded:
The heartbeat over a hundred and forty, the basketball bump, the lunar calendar tested on 2.8 million births, timing and cereal, the ring on a thread, and the one piece of folklore that is partly true.

The sex-prediction folklore, each myth against the study that tested it. Where your baby is: Carnegie stage 23, ~30 mm, the last day of the embryonic period, with SRY switching the gonads at 6–7 weeks post-fertilization and the external anatomy not yet readable. The sex ratio at conception is 0.5 (Orzack 2015), so every method is right half the time. Heart rate: no sex difference in 212 pregnancies across 2,261 visits (Genuis 1996) or in 477 first-trimester scans (girls 151.7 vs boys 154.9 bpm; McKenna 2006) — it tracks age, not sex. Bump shape and morning-sickness folklore failed in 104 women (Perry 1999), and maternal intuition was no better than chance (Genuis 1996). The Chinese lunar calendar on 2,840,755 Swedish births: kappa 0.0002 (Villamor 2010). Timing of intercourse made no difference (Wilcox 1995, NEJM). The breakfast-cereal finding (Mathews 2008) was most likely a multiple-testing false positive (Young 2009). The ring on a thread, urine chemistry (and the drain-cleaner hazard) and the six-week placenta method have no published validation. The partly true one: severe sickness is linked to girls (54.1% vs 48.7% overall; Mitsuda 2019; Askling 1999) — a real association and still a nearly useless predictor.

Today's action: For fun: tonight each of you writes a boy/girl guess and the method behind it (heartbeat, bump, dream, calendar, a real coin toss); add two grandparents' guesses and methods. Seal them in an envelope dated Day 69, put it in the back of the Day 61 pregnancy file, and open it the day you find out.

The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 68 · Week 9 — Protocol: screening decisions as a couple
item.description:
Every test on one calendar, the detection rates, why a positive screen is never a diagnosis, the needle risk as it's measured now, who wants to know the sex, and a seven-line worksheet.
The Protocol episode that turns Days 59, 65 and 66 into a decision. The testing window opens on Day 70: carrier screening, cell-free DNA from 10 weeks, the nuchal scan and combined screen at 11–13+6 weeks, CVS at 10–13 weeks, amniocentesis from 15 weeks, the quad screen at 15–22 weeks and the anatomy scan at ~20 weeks. ACOG Practice Bulletin 226: every patient offered both screening and diagnostic testing, with the right to decline. The scoreboard for trisomy 21 (quad 81%, combined 82–87%, integrated/sequential 95–96%, cfDNA 99%; Gil 2017: 99.7% detection, 0.04% false positives across 35 studies). Why a positive screen is an instruction to get a diagnosis, not a diagnosis. The needle risk recalculated: Akolekar 2015 (0.11% amniocentesis, 0.22% CVS) and Salomon 2019 (0.30% and 0.20%, falling to 0.12% and ~0 in risk-matched studies), against the one-in-two-hundred still quoted; CEMAT 1998 and why amniocentesis waits until 15 weeks (clubfoot 1.3% vs 0.1%). The three reasons couples test, and declining as a fourth legitimate position. Fetal sex: cfDNA accuracy by week (Devaney 2011), ultrasound at 12–14 weeks (Efrat 2006), the sex-chromosome caveat, and the four disclosure arrangements.
Today's action: Twenty minutes together before Day 70: one page, seven lines — (1) carrier screening status/result; (2) cfDNA yes/no, cost, draw week; (3) nuchal scan yes/no and booking between Day 77 and 97; (4) if high-chance, CVS or amniocentesis?; (5) the first sentence each of you would say if a diagnosis were confirmed; (6) sex: both know / neither / one / envelope, and whether sex-chromosome results are reported; (7) who gets the phone call. File it behind the Questions page of the Day 61 pregnancy file.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 67 · Week 9 — Adventure: cold-weather sport without falls
item.description:
One pregnant woman in four falls, one in two thousand is admitted, the pelvis that guards the first trimester, the sport with a tenth of the injuries, and the twenty-dollar cleat.
Winter's risk isn't the cold, it's the ground. The ACOG exercise guidance (150 minutes a week; continue vigorous exercise if already active) and its exceptions — ice hockey, downhill skiing and other fall-prone sports — with cross-country skiing, snowshoeing and walking absent from the list. How often pregnant women fall (26.8% of 3,997 in the NIOSH-funded Dunning study, two-thirds of work falls from slippery floors, hurrying or carrying), why (balance stable at 11–14 weeks, worse from the second trimester and still impaired 6–8 weeks postpartum, with growing reliance on vision — Butler 2006), and what a fall does (Schiff 2008: 48.9 hospitalisations per 100,000 deliveries, 79% in the third trimester and 9% in the first; abruption RR 8.0, preterm labour RR 4.4). Why the first trimester is the forgiving window — the uterus is still behind the pelvic girdle. Slope numbers: 1.5–6 injuries per 1,000 alpine skier days, cross-country about a tenth of that, helmets cutting head injury by about a third. A randomised trial in which slip-on traction devices cut outdoor winter falls from 43 to 19. The after-a-fall rules, including monitoring after an abdominal fall from 20 weeks and anti-D for Rh-negative women.
Today's action: Order slip-on traction cleats in your partner's shoe size and your own and put them by the door before the first ice. On the Questions page of the Day 61 file add 'After a fall': bleeding, pain, fluid, fainting or a blow to the belly → same-day call; from 20 weeks any fall onto the belly → monitoring; her blood group is ___. If a ski trip is booked, add question eighteen with the week and sleeping altitude.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 66 · Week 9 — Parents: screening season
item.description:
The tentative pregnancy, the anxiety curve after a positive, the false alarms cell-free DNA abolished, the roles men get handed, and who decides.
The human side of yesterday's physiology. From now to the anatomy scan, couples live through a sequence of tests with waits attached — what Barbara Katz Rothman called the tentative pregnancy. The measured anxiety curve after a positive screen in both partners (Burton 1985, including 148 male partners; Marteau 1992), the 2004 Health Technology Assessment review of 106 studies (anxiety falls with reassurance but may leave a residue; the all-clear has not been shown to reassure; up to 30% regret), a small signal that a false alarm may touch early mother–infant interaction (Viaux-Savelon 2012, n=19), and the biggest change of all: cell-free DNA cut false alarms from about 54 per thousand couples to under one (NEXT, 2015). The father specifically: the roles Locock and Alexander named (parent, bystander, protector, guardian of fact, decider/enforcer), the 18-study metasynthesis showing involved men become more engaged, and 4–16% of expectant fathers with an anxiety disorder (Leach 2016). Who decides — she has the final say, you have a real say — and the Cochrane evidence (105 trials, 31,043 people) that structured decision aids raise knowledge and values-congruent choices without raising anxiety. Four practical rules: the phone plan, the first question after any result, protecting the pregnancy during the wait, and choosing your role out loud.
Today's action: Fifteen minutes tonight. Each of you separately finishes two sentences — 'If a screening result came back high-risk, the first thing I'd want is…' and 'The thing I'd most want you to do in that moment is…' — then swap and read without debating. Agree the phone plan (who gets the call, whether the other must be present) and write it on the Questions page of the Day 61 file next to question seventeen.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 65 · Week 9 — Physiology: the placenta is in her blood
item.description:
Cell-free DNA, the man who found it looking for cells, why the test waits for ten weeks, the fetal fraction her weight dilutes, the ninety-nine point seven that is real, the positive predictive value that depends on her age, the results that found cancer in the mother, and the cup of coffee that now lasts eight hours.
Week 9, Day 2 is post-fertilization day 51, Carnegie stage 21 (22–24 mm), the stage at which the cortical plate emerges. Today is the physiology behind cell-free DNA screening (NIPT). Placental DNA circulates in the mother's plasma: found by Lo in 1997 in 80% of women carrying boys; shown by Alberry 2007 to come from the trophoblast, not the fetus (normal levels in anembryonic pregnancies); cleared with a 16-minute half-life (Lo 1999), so the reading is live. Fetal fraction is a median 10% at 10 weeks (Wang 2013, 22,384 pregnancies), which is why the test waits until Day 70; it falls with maternal weight, from 11.7% at 60 kg to 3.9% at 160 kg, with 7.1% of women at 100 kg below the 4% floor (Ashoor 2013), and 56% of failed draws succeed on redraw. Counting performance for trisomy 21: 99.7% detection, 0.04% false positives (Gil 2017); in 15,841 routine pregnancies cfDNA found 38/38 Down syndrome cases vs 30/38 for standard screening, with 0.06% vs 5.4% false positives and a positive predictive value of 80.9% vs 3.4% (Norton 2015, NEXT). PPV depends on maternal age: from Morris 2002 and Snijders 1999 baselines with Gil's rates, roughly 70% at 25, 78% at 30, 90% at 35, 97% at 40 — and far lower for the sex chromosome conditions. False positives come from confined placental mosaicism, maternal copy-number variants, vanished twins and maternal cancer (Hartwig 2017); multiple-aneuploidy patterns flagged cancer in 18% of such results (Bianchi 2015) and 48.6% of women with unusual or non-reportable results had an occult cancer on whole-body MRI (Turriff 2024). A no-call is followed up, not ignored (ACOG PB 226). Sex from Y-chromosome fragments: 95–99% sensitivity depending on gestation (Devaney 2011). Coda: caffeine half-life rises from 3.4 to 8.3 hours in pregnancy (Knutti 1981; Yu 2016).
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, and nothing to decide. One: on the Questions page of the Day 61 file, add question seventeen in three parts: 'Do you offer cell-free DNA screening, from which week do you draw it, and does the lab report fetal fraction and its no-call policy?' Two: on the same page, write the line that will matter if a result comes back: 'A positive means the chance, at her age, is about ___ percent; a confirmatory test is CVS or amniocentesis; a no-call is followed up, not ignored.' Leave the blank for the OB or fill it from today's numbers. Three: if your partner's weight is over about 100 kg, write 'draw at 11–12 weeks, not 10' beside the question, with Ashoor's 7% as the reason. The deciding — whether to have it, what you'd do with it, who wants to know the sex — is the Day 68 Protocol episode. Tonight is only the understanding.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

Two: on the same page, write the line that will matter if a result comes back: 'A positive means the chance, at her age, is about ___ percent; a confirmatory test is CVS or amniocentesis; a no-call is followed up, not ignored.' Leave the blank for the OB or fill it from today's numbers. Three: if your partner's weight is over about 100 kg, write 'draw at 11–12 weeks, not 10' beside the question, with Ashoor's 7% as the reason. The deciding — whether to have it, what you'd do with it, who wants to know the sex — is the Day 68 Protocol episode. Tonight is only the understanding.

item.title: Day 64 · Week 9 — Brain: the plate
item.description:
The first layer of the thinking brain appears this week, the ropes the neurons climb, the inside-out rule, the waiting room that is bigger in humans than in anything else, the ear that closes its coil, and the virus in toddler saliva that only a father's hands can keep out.
Week 9, Day 1 is post-fertilization day 50, the turn from Carnegie stage 20 to 21 (20–24 mm). The Day 57 neuron factory now has a destination: the cortical plate, the embryonic cortex, which Meyer's 2000 human series shows emerging at stage 21, within a day or two of today. Neurons born at the ventricular surface climb radial glial fibres (Rakic 1972, 1988) and settle inside-out, deepest layers first (Angevine & Sidman 1961). Beneath the plate a transient subplate forms, the thalamic axons' waiting room, larger in humans than in any other species (Kostović & Judaš 2010; Molnár 2019). The cochlea completes its coil this week, hair cells differentiate at 10–12 weeks, function begins at 18–20 weeks, and the first behavioural responses to sound appear at 19 weeks (Pujol 1991; Hepper & Shahidullah 1994). Three things with human evidence reach the climbing neurons: alcohol, whose mechanism is disrupted proliferation and migration (Miller 1986) and whose US burden is 1.1–5.0% of first-graders (May 2018); valproate, 11 IQ points at age 6 (Meador 2013) and 9.8% malformations (Cochrane 2023); and cytomegalovirus, which infects 1 in 200 newborns and leaves 1 in 5 of them with permanent problems, mostly hearing (CDC), is caught from the saliva and urine of young children, and against which a hygiene briefing cut new maternal infections from 7.6% to 1.2% (Revello 2015). The father's lever: take the toddler's diapers, plates and pacifiers until Day 280.
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, in two parts. One: answer the toddler question out loud with your partner — is there a child under five she will be handling regularly between now and Day 280 (yours, a niece or nephew, a classroom, a nursery, a ward)? If no, write 'CMV: low exposure' on the Us page of the Day 61 file and move on. If yes, write Revello's list under it: soap after diapers and noses; no shared cups, cutlery, food, toothbrushes or pacifiers; no kisses on the mouth; no co-sleeping with the toddler — and in your handwriting, 'diapers, potty, plates, pacifiers: his.' Two: add question sixteen to the Day 40 list: 'Given her exposure to young children, should she have a CMV antibody test, and what would you do with either answer?' Bring it to the next visit.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 63 · Week 9 — Body: the first choreography
item.description:
The embryo has been moving for a week, the one-second bend from the spinal cord, the general movement that means the brain has joined in, the hiccup on a three-second clock, and why she'll feel none of it until Day 112.
Week 9 opens the last full week of the embryonic period. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 20 (post-fertilization day 49; 18–22 mm): fingers separated by programmed cell death, toes forming, an elbow, a pigmented eye with the first eyelid fold, an ear canal, the liver bulging, the trunk straightening and the head lifting, a vascular network under the scalp; stages 21–23 follow by Day 70 (hands meeting, the tail going, head half the body, 'external genital primordium developing'). The arm nerves are already in adult arrangement (Shinohara 1990, 8 embryos). The heart peaks at about 170 bpm at 9–10 weeks (Doubilet & Benson 1995; Papaioannou 2010, 4,698 pregnancies) and a normal early heartbeat carries 91.4% first-trimester success (Doubilet & Guo 2024). The main event: spontaneous movement, from the Groningen films (de Vries, Visser & Prechtl 1982, 1985, 1988; 11–12 women scanned an hour a week from 7 weeks) and the IVF series (Lüchinger 2008; 18 embryos). First movements at 7.5 weeks — a one-second sideways bend of head or rump, generated by spinal cord and brainstem; arms and legs joining by 8.5 weeks; general movements from 8–9 weeks (whole-body, varying in speed, force and direction — the signature of supraspinal modulation, i.e. the brain joining in; sideways bends fall at 9 weeks, p=0.01, general movements rise, p=0.006); startles; hiccups from about 9 weeks at a preferred interval of 1–3 seconds; isolated arm movements about one a second; then head movements, hand–face contact, breathing movements from 10 weeks (rhythm shifting from one per 2–3 s to under 1 s by 19 weeks), jaw opening, stretch, yawn, sucking and swallowing by 12.5 weeks; all 16 patterns present in every fetus by 15 weeks. Between 8 and 19 weeks the longest stillness was 13 minutes; no male–female difference in any pattern, but consistent individual differences in activity. Unlike Hooker's filmed reflex (Day 57), these need no stimulus. Why she feels nothing: a 20 mm body in a fist-sized uterus below the pubic bone; quickening at 16–22 weeks (Day 112–154; Day 153 coming). The nine-week scan: CRL curves (Robinson; Hadlock 1992, 416 women, ±8%; Pexsters 2010, 3,710 pregnancies) agree at 9 weeks; ACOG CO 700 redating only if >7 days apart; movement is reliably visible now — ask to watch for twenty seconds; and sex cannot be read yet (genital tubercle indifferent; tubercle-angle technique at 11–14 weeks; Day 69 Myths coming). The cochlear duct completes its 2.5 turns by the end of the embryonic period; hearing itself is Day 161.
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, and one request at the scan. One: on the Dates page of the Day 61 file, add three lines — 'movement began: about Day 52, unfelt'; 'quickening window: Day 112 to Day 154'; and beside the scan date, the Day 56 rule, 'CRL replaces the period date only if more than seven days apart'. Two: at this week's scan, after the measurement, ask the sonographer: 'Can we watch for twenty seconds and see it move?' If it does, write 'movement seen, Day ___' on the back of the Day 42 card under the heart rate; if it doesn't, write '13 min' beside it, the longest it would have stayed still. Three: if the scan has already happened and nobody looked, nothing is lost — the next one shows more, and Day 153 is where movement starts to matter.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 62 · Week 8 — Myths: the scan cooks the baby and the Doppler should be refused, a fright or a row can end a pregnancy, and a positive on the…
item.description:
The fifth Myths episode, closing Week 8 with the folklore of the first visit. Your baby is at the end of Carnegie stage 19 (about 18 mm): trunk straightening, head lifting, hands drifting toward each other over the heart. Myth one, the scan heats the baby: the half that's true (ultrasound is energy; the thermal index on every screen estimates worst-case warming, TI 1 ≈ 1 °C; the FDA caps output at 720 mW/cm² and MI 1.9), the thresholds (≤1.5 °C above normal 'without reservation'; 41 °C for 5 min is the hazard line; B-mode runs at TI well under 0.7, where BMUS sets no time limit, then a clock: 60 min at TI ≤1, 30 at ≤1.5, 15 at ≤2, 4 at ≤2.5), and the outcomes: the WHO systematic review (Torloni 2009; 41 studies, 61 publications) found no adverse maternal, perinatal, growth, neurological, cancer or cognitive outcome — only a weak non-right-handedness signal in boys (OR 1.26; Salvesen 2011 pooled 8,865 trial children, OR 1.15); Newnham's RCT (1993; 2,834 women, five scans with Doppler vs one) found more small babies (RR 1.35) and its 8-year follow-up (2004; 2,714 children) found identical size by age one and no developmental difference at any age; Cochrane 2015 (11 trials, 37,505 women) on routine early scans. The half-right part: pulsed Doppler delivers more energy, so WFUMB/ISUOG (2015) say no routine first-trimester Doppler, TI ≤1.0, 5–10 min; the FDA (2014) discourages keepsake scans and home Dopplers while noting no evidence of harm; the real home-Doppler danger is third-trimester false reassurance (Tommy's, Kicks Count). Myth two, stress ends pregnancies: chromosomal error is the largest cause of early loss (Hardy 2016, 40 years of karyotypes, rising with maternal age); the stress meta-analysis (Qu 2017; 8 studies; OR 1.42, 1.19–1.70; work stress 1.27) leans on a postal case-control asked after the loss (Maconochie 2007; 603 cases, 6,116 controls); the prospective studies split — Nelson 2003 (326 women, three scales plus cortisol, no association; stress predicted smoking and cannabis) vs Schliep 2022 (797 EAGeR women with a prior loss; HR 1.69 for any loss, 1.58 and crossing 1 for clinical loss); Nepomnaschy 2006 cortisol (emerging); shift work (Bonde 2013: fixed nights RR 1.51, 40–52 h weeks 1.36, 'reassuring'). The honest size: chronic months-long stress, never a fright or a row, and a 1.4× multiplier on this week's few-percent baseline (Doubilet & Guo 2024: 91.4% success after a normal early heartbeat, 93.8% without risk factors). Myth three, a positive on the bloods is a verdict: hepatitis B — vaccine 75%, vaccine plus HBIG 94% effective (CDC), tenofovir from 30 weeks for high viral load (Pan 2016 NEJM; 200 mothers; 5% vs 18% ITT, 0 vs 7% per…
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight with the Day 61 file open to two pages. The fifth Myths episode, closing Week 8 with the folklore of the first visit. Your baby is at the end of Carnegie stage 19 (about 18 mm): trunk straightening, head lifting, hands drifting toward each other over the heart. Myth one, the scan heats the baby: the half that's true (ultrasound is energy; the thermal index on every screen estimates worst-case warming, TI 1 ≈ 1 °C; the FDA caps output at 720 mW/cm² and MI 1.9), the thresholds (≤1.5 °C above normal 'without reservation'; 41 °C for 5 min is the hazard line; B-mode runs at TI well under 0.7, where BMUS sets no time limit, then a clock: 60 min at TI ≤1, 30 at ≤1.5, 15 at ≤2, 4 at ≤2.5), and the outcomes: the WHO systematic review (Torloni 2009; 41 studies, 61 publications) found no adverse maternal, perinatal, growth, neurological, cancer or cognitive outcome — only a weak non-right-handedness signal in boys (OR 1.26; Salvesen 2011 pooled 8,865 trial children, OR 1.15); Newnham's RCT (1993; 2,834 women, five scans with Doppler vs one) found more small babies (RR 1.35) and its 8-year follow-up (2004; 2,714 children) found identical size by age one and no developmental difference at any age; Cochrane 2015 (11 trials, 37,505 women) on routine early scans. The half-right part: pulsed Doppler delivers more energy, so WFUMB/ISUOG (2015) say no routine first-trimester Doppler, TI ≤1.0, 5–10 min; the FDA (2014) discourages keepsake scans and home Dopplers while noting no evidence of harm; the real home-Doppler danger is third-trimester false reassurance (Tommy's, Kicks Count). Myth two, stress ends pregnancies: chromosomal error is the largest cause of early loss (Hardy 2016, 40 years of karyotypes, rising with maternal age); the stress meta-analysis (Qu 2017; 8 studies; OR 1.42, 1.19–1.70; work stress 1.27) leans on a postal case-control asked after the loss (Maconochie 2007; 603 cases, 6,116 controls); the prospective studies split — Nelson 2003 (326 women, three scales plus cortisol, no association; stress predicted smoking and cannabis) vs Schliep 2022 (797 EAGeR women with a prior loss; HR 1.69 for any loss, 1.58 and crossing 1 for clinical loss); Nepomnaschy 2006 cortisol (emerging); shift work (Bonde 2013: fixed nights RR 1.51, 40–52 h weeks 1.36, 'reassuring'). The honest size: chronic months-long stress, never a fright or a row, and a 1.4× multiplier on this week's few-percent baseline (Doubilet & Guo 2024: 91.4% success after a normal early heartbeat, 93.8% without risk factors). item.title: Day 61 · Week 8 — Protocol: the pregnancy file
item.description:
Five sections, every first-visit number with its threshold, the women who carried their own notes, and the law that makes the results hers the moment they exist.
The fifth Protocol episode, and the folder the loose pages since Day 35 go into. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 19 (16–18 mm), trunk lengthening, head lifting, elbows bent with the hands meeting — and about to be measured crown to rump for the first time. Why a record she holds: Cochrane 2015 (Brown et al.; 4 trials, 1,176 women): women carrying their own notes felt in control (RR 1.56, 1.18–2.06), wanted to carry them again (RR 1.79), lost them no more often — and the honest odd signal of more caesareans (RR 1.51) and operative deliveries (RR 1.83) in two single trials; NICE NG201 on updating the record at every visit. Section one, dates: LMP, cycle, the Day 28 due date, CRL and the ACOG CO 700 redating rule; the schedule — US monthly/fortnightly/weekly, 12–14 visits codified in 1930 (Peahl & Howell 2021), NICE's 10 appointments for a first pregnancy and 7 thereafter with two scans, WHO's 8 contacts. Section two, the numbers with thresholds: blood pressure as the baseline (ALSPAC, 13,016 women: later-hypertensive women already higher at 8 weeks — Macdonald-Wallis 2012), 140/90 on two readings 4 h apart, 160/110 same-day (ACOG, NICE), pre-eclampsia ~4% US (USPSTF 2017, grade B for BP at every visit) and up to 8% globally, aspirin 81 mg from 12–28 weeks for risk factors, and the BUMP trials (Tucker, Chappell 2022: 2,441 and 850 women; self-monitoring detected hypertension no earlier and controlled it no better); IOM 2009 weight bands by BMI; the Day 50 blood-count lines (Hb 11, ferritin 30, MCV, platelets); blood group, Rh and the 28-week antibody repeat; the four infection screens with their reasons — hepatitis B (≈17,800 US infants a year born to carriers, 0.5% of births; ~90% of perinatally infected infants chronic, a quarter of those dying of liver disease — CDC), HIV (15–45% transmission untreated — WHO), syphilis (3,882 congenital cases and 279 stillbirths/infant deaths in 2023; ~40% of babies of untreated mothers stillborn or dying — CDC), rubella (Miller 1982: defects in every infected infant before week 11, 35% at 13–16 weeks, none after 16); urine culture — 2–10% prevalence, USPSTF 2019 grade B, Cochrane 2019 (15 trials: pyelonephritis RR 0.24, low birth weight RR 0.64, low certainty) against Kazemier 2015 (4,283 women: untreated bacteriuria pyelonephritis 2.4% vs 0.6%, no preterm excess). What isn't routine (TSH, vitamin D). Section three, the pages already made. Section four, how data arrives: Cures Act immediate release since 5 April 2021, HIPAA's 30 days, and Steitz 2023 (8,139…
Today's action: Twenty minutes tonight: building, not reading. One: a folder with five dividers, or a shared note on both phones with five headings — Dates, Numbers, Questions, Medicines, Us. Two: fill Dates from what you have: last period, cycle length, the Day 28 due date, the Day 40 scan date, and the appointment schedule you're on (two scans, the 24–28-week glucose test and the 27–36-week vaccine window pencilled in). Three: on Numbers, write the left-hand column and thresholds before any results exist — blood pressure (140/90; 160/110), weight and BMI with her IOM band, haemoglobin (11), ferritin (30), blood group and Rh with your type beside it, hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis, rubella immunity, chlamydia, urine culture, crown-rump length with the dating rule — and leave the right-hand column blank. Four: move the Day 40 sheet, the Day 42 card, the Day 54 medication list and the Day 60 insurance page into their dividers, and write the Day 28 after-hours number on the cover. Five: at this week's visit, ask how results are released, whether there is a portal and whether she wants you on it, and ask for a printed copy of the booking bloods. Then photograph every page.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 60 · Week 8 — Adventure: the long-haul
item.description:
One clot in four and a half thousand flights, the stocking that stops nine in ten, the eleven percent on the Zika map, mefloquine or elsewhere, and the clause nobody reads.
The fifth Adventure episode: Day 32 cleared the short flight; today is the twelve-hour one and the far-away country. Your baby is at the turn of Carnegie stage 18 to 19 (16–18 mm), trunk straightening, hands and feet reaching toward the midline — and reached by an airplane only through your partner's body. Permission: ACOG CO 746 (occasional air travel safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy; seat belt on; cosmic radiation negligible), airlines to 36 weeks and cruise lines to 24 (CDC Yellow Book), some airlines wanting a letter from 28 weeks and some insurers stopping at 32 (EBCOG 2022); 628,292 Israeli births with +9 g and +0.36 days for the 6.6% who flew (Shalev Ram 2020); flight attendants' OR 1.3 (0.9–1.8) (Aspholm 1999); ten wired women with normal fetal heart rates in the air (Huch 1986). The cabin: 1,800–2,500 m equivalent, below the Day 46 sleeping line; SpO2 90–95%; the Hb <8, sickle-cell and cardiopulmonary exceptions; humidity under 10%; a 10-hour flight ≈ 0.05 mGy, half a chest X-ray against the Day 57 50-mGy line. The clot: baseline VTE 0.5–2 per 1,000 pregnancies, 4–5× the non-pregnant rate, 9.3% of US maternal deaths (ACOG PB 196); Kuipers 2007 (8,755 employees, 38,910 person-years, 53 clots): IRR 3.2 after flights ≥4 h, one event per 4,656 long-haul flights, ~1 in 1,264 over 16 h, +10% per hour, +40% per extra flight; MEGA (Cannegieter 2006): pregnancy plus flight OR 14.3, window seat vs aisle OR 2.2; combined, roughly 1 in 1,000 per flight with wide uncertainty — and Cochrane 2021 (12 trials, 2,918 passengers): symptomless DVT 3 vs 47, OR 0.10, high certainty; RCOG stockings for every pregnant woman over 4 h; BSH 2023's 4-hour definition and pregnancy as a risk factor; LMWH only with extra risk factors. Time zones: melatonin works for adults crossing ≥5 zones (Cochrane 2002, NNT ~2) but the NHS says not in pregnancy, so fly west, use daylight, empty the first day. The map: CDC's rule against travel to an active Zika notice; Honein 2017 (442 pregnancies: 6% birth defects, 11% first trimester, same whether symptomatic; baseline microcephaly 7 per 10,000); Brasil 2016 (42% of 117 live infants abnormal; 55% adverse after first-trimester infection); condoms for the whole pregnancy after a partner's exposure. Malaria: worse in pregnancy (Yellow Book); 125.2 million pregnancies a year in transmission areas (Dellicour 2010); 12.4 million African women exposed and 900,000 low-birth-weight babies a year, 65% of placental infections first taking hold at the end of the first trimester (Walker…
Today's action: Fifteen minutes tonight with the long-haul booking open. One: her seat is an aisle on every leg, and the below-the-knee graduated compression stockings from Day 32 are in the house in her calf size — order them now if not. Two: ask the travel insurer four questions, in writing: does the policy cover complications of pregnancy abroad, including miscarriage, and to what week; does it cover a premature baby's care abroad; does it include medical evacuation and to where; is anything in her history excluded as pre-existing. Write the answers with the policy number on one page; a no or a vague answer is the thing to fix before anything non-refundable is paid. Three: open the CDC travel pages for the destination — an active Zika notice means she doesn't go; malaria means a travel-clinic appointment three to four weeks out with 'pregnant' as the first word (mefloquine or chloroquine only). Four: look up the altitude of the arrival city and hotel; above 2,750 m, the Day 46 rule applies. Then write the name and address of the nearest hospital with an obstetric unit at the destination on the same page. That page goes in the pregnancy file — tomorrow's Protocol.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

Permission: ACOG CO 746 (occasional air travel safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy; seat belt on; cosmic radiation negligible), airlines to 36 weeks and cruise lines to 24 (CDC Yellow Book), some airlines wanting a letter from 28 weeks and some insurers stopping at 32 (EBCOG 2022); 628,292 Israeli births with +9 g and +0.36 days for the 6.6% who flew (Shalev Ram 2020); flight attendants' OR 1.3 (0.9–1.8) (Aspholm 1999); ten wired women with normal fetal heart rates in the air (Huch 1986). The cabin: 1,800–2,500 m equivalent, below the Day 46 sleeping line; SpO2 90–95%; the Hb <8, sickle-cell and cardiopulmonary exceptions; humidity under 10%; a 10-hour flight ≈ 0.05 mGy, half a chest X-ray against the Day 57 50-mGy line. The clot: baseline VTE 0.5–2 per 1,000 pregnancies, 4–5× the non-pregnant rate, 9.3% of US maternal deaths (ACOG PB 196); Kuipers 2007 (8,755 employees, 38,910 person-years, 53 clots): IRR 3.2 after flights ≥4 h, one event per 4,656 long-haul flights, ~1 in 1,264 over 16 h, +10% per hour, +40% per extra flight; MEGA (Cannegieter 2006): pregnancy plus flight OR 14.3, window seat vs aisle OR 2.2; combined, roughly 1 in 1,000 per flight with wide uncertainty — and Cochrane 2021 (12 trials, 2,918 passengers): symptomless DVT 3 vs 47, OR 0.10, high certainty; RCOG stockings for every pregnant woman over 4 h; BSH 2023's 4-hour definition and pregnancy as a risk factor; LMWH only with extra risk factors. Time zones: melatonin works for adults crossing ≥5 zones (Cochrane 2002, NNT ~2) but the NHS says not in pregnancy, so fly west, use daylight, empty the first day. The map: CDC's rule against travel to an active Zika notice; Honein 2017 (442 pregnancies: 6% birth defects, 11% first trimester, same whether symptomatic; baseline microcephaly 7 per 10,000); Brasil 2016 (42% of 117 live infants abnormal; 55% adverse after first-trimester infection); condoms for the whole pregnancy after a partner's exposure. Malaria: worse in pregnancy (Yellow Book); 125.2 million pregnancies a year in transmission areas (Dellicour 2010); 12.4 million African women exposed and 900,000 low-birth-weight babies a year, 65% of placental infections first taking hold at the end of the first trimester (Walker…

Today's action: Fifteen minutes tonight with the long-haul booking open. One: her seat is an aisle on every leg, and the below-the-knee graduated compression stockings from Day 32 are in the house in her calf size — order them now if not. Two: ask the travel insurer four questions, in writing: does the policy cover complications of pregnancy abroad, including miscarriage, and to what week; does it cover a premature baby's care abroad; does it include medical evacuation and to where; is anything in her history excluded as pre-existing. Write the answers with the policy number on one page; a no or a vague answer is the thing to fix before anything non-refundable is paid. Three: open the CDC travel pages for the destination — an active Zika notice means she doesn't go; malaria means a travel-clinic appointment three to four weeks out with 'pregnant' as the first word (mefloquine or chloroquine only). Four: look up the altitude of the arrival city and hotel; above 2,750 m, the Day 46 rule applies. Then write the name and address of the nearest hospital with an obstetric unit at the destination on the same page. That page goes in the pregnancy file — tomorrow's Protocol.

The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 59 · Week 8 — Parents: the test that's about you too
item.description:
Carrier screening, the one in twenty-five, what your age writes into the genome, and what ten thousand couples did with the answer.
The fifth Parents episode, paying question three on the Day 40 sheet. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 18 (13–17 mm), the clavicle's two bone centres merging today, elbows bent, toe rays appearing — and every cell carrying a genome finished on Day 14, half hers and half yours. What a carrier is and why neither of you would know; Mendel's one in four, every pregnancy. Who is offered what: ACOG CO 690/691 (information to every pregnant woman, ideally preconception; cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy and haemoglobinopathies to all; partner tested if she's positive; any of it may be declined) and ACMG 2021 (a single ~113-condition panel for everyone, ancestry-based screening retired). The numbers: CF 1 in 2,500–3,500 white newborns, 1 in 17,000 African American, 1 in 31,000 Asian American (MedlinePlus), ~1 carrier in 25 of Northern European descent (ACOG) — and the arithmetic that closes; SMA 1 carrier in 54 pan-ethnic, 1/47 to 1/72 by ancestry, 91% detection, 1 baby in 11,000 (Sugarman 2012, 72,453 samples), the 3–4% of carriers a copy-number test misses, treatments since 2016; sickle cell trait in 1 in 13 Black babies, disease in 1 in 365 Black and 1 in 16,300 Hispanic births (CDC), screened through the CBC and electrophoresis, and the NHS programme's explicit next step: test the biological father. Fragile X (1 in 4,000 males, 1 in 8,000 females; 55–200-repeat premutations expanding only through the mother) and Tay-Sachs (1 in 30 Ashkenazi vs 1 in 300). How wide to cast the net: Haque 2016 (346,790 people; 94–392 at-risk fetuses per 100,000 by ancestry; guideline panels catching 6–87% of what the expanded panel finds). What a result does to a couple: Mackenzie's Mission (Kirk 2024, NEJM; 10,038 couples, ≥1,281 genes; 1.9% newly at increased chance; 76.6% used or planned an intervention; more anxiety, low regret, 98.9% acceptability). The father's share: ~2 new mutations per year of paternal age (Kong 2012, 78 trios), autism RR 5.75 for fathers ≥40 (Reichenberg 2006) and 1.66 for fathers ≥50 vs twenties in 5.77 million children (Sandin 2016) — about 1 in 190 moving toward 1 in 110. And your blood type: Rh D negative in ~15% of Europeans (ACOG PB 181), anti-D prevention (MedlinePlus), and the 373,300 cases of Rh disease still occurring worldwide in 2010 (Bhutani 2013).
Today's action: Fifteen minutes tonight, together, with the Day 40 question sheet. One: decide whether you want carrier screening and, if so, ask for both of you to be tested at once — rewrite question three as 'We'd like carrier screening; which panel do you offer, can we both be tested now, and how long do results take?' Two: put both family-history sheets side by side; note anything that recurs on either side, any ancestry that puts a condition on the list, and any blood relation between the two of you. Three: write your blood type next to hers under question six, or the plan to find it out this week. Then say one sentence out loud before folding the sheet: 'If we're both carriers of something, here's roughly what we'd want to do.' You don't have to agree tonight; you have to have started.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.
