item.title: Day 58 · Week 8 — Physiology: her mouth
item.description:
The bacterium that eats her hormones, the three trials that killed a seven-fold risk, and the bugs your child will catch from her at two.
The fifth Physiology episode. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 18 (13–17 mm; the NHS raspberry), the tibia's shaft turning to bone today behind the clavicle and femur, the elbow bending — and in a jaw the size of a rice grain, the dental lamina and the first twenty tooth buds forming (Hovorakova 2018), to mineralise from ~14 weeks (Lunt & Law 1974). Pregnancy gingivitis: 60–75% of pregnant women (CDC), peaking in the third trimester (ACOG CO 569), named by Löe & Silness 1963; inflammation rises through pregnancy without a rise in plaque (Figuero 2013, 33 studies). Why: leakier gum vessels, and Prevotella intermedia, which can substitute oestradiol or progesterone for vitamin K and grows on her hormones (Kornman & Loesche 1980, 1982; Jensen 1981). It is reversible and does not progress to periodontitis (Gürsoy 2008). Pregnancy epulis in ~5%; acid from vomiting is rinsed, not brushed, for an hour. Then the great story: a 7.5-fold odds ratio for preterm low birth weight (Offenbacher 1996, 124 women), 18 of 25 observational studies agreeing (Xiong 2006), 11.2% vs 28.6% preterm in OCAP (Offenbacher 2006, 1,020 women) — and three large randomised trials of deep cleaning in pregnancy that moved nothing: OPT (Michalowicz 2006, 823 women, 12.0% vs 12.8%), MOTOR (Offenbacher 2009, 1,806 women, 13.1% vs 11.5%), PIPS (Macones 2010, 757 women, RR 1.19), and the Cochrane review of 15 trials and 7,161 women (preterm RR 0.87, 0.70–1.10; no adverse effects). Why the dentist still matters: 40–50% of pregnant women have periodontal disease and 56% see no dentist; ACOG says X-rays with shielding and lidocaine are safe and treatment should not be delayed (Hagai 2015: 210 exposed pregnancies, anomalies 4.8% vs 3.3%, NS); free NHS dental care through a year after the due date. And the finding that outlasted the preterm hypothesis: decay is infectious, children acquire mutans streptococci in a window around 26 months (Caufield 1993), 71% from an identical maternal strain and never the father's (Li & Caufield 1995), children of mothers with untreated decay >3× more likely to have cavities (CDC) — and the Finnish xylitol trial (Söderling 2000; Isokangas 2000: colonisation 9.7% vs 28.6–48.5%, decay at five down ~70%). Plus the truth behind 'a tooth for every child' (Russell 2010: more untreated, not more total, decay).
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: she books a dental check-up and cleaning for this trimester, says she's pregnant when booking, and asks for the usual X-rays with shielding; if the practice hesitates, the sentence is 'ACOG and the ADA say dental care in pregnancy is safe and should not be delayed.' In England, ask for the FW8 maternity exemption form at the booking appointment — the dentist is free through a year after the due date. Two: a box of baking soda and a cup go by the bathroom sink tonight, with the rule said once: after being sick, rinse, don't brush, for an hour. Optional: a packet of xylitol gum in the kitchen drawer for the habit the Finnish trial started after the birth.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 57 · Week 8 — Brain: the factory opens
item.description:
A hundred and seventy thousand neurons a minute from yesterday to Day 122, the first reflex ever filmed, and the dose of a chest X-ray against the line the bombs drew.
The fifth Brain episode. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 18 (13–17 mm; the NHS raspberry), the femur's shaft turning to bone today by the Keibel & Mall timetable, the hemispheres hollow bubbles whose walls are almost entirely factory. The schedule from Stiles & Jernigan 2010: neural progenitors in the ventricular zone divide symmetrically from embryonic day 25 to 42 (Day 39–56), doubling the pool; from E42 — yesterday — division turns asymmetric and each round yields a neuron that will never divide again; neocortical neurogenesis is essentially complete by about E108 (Day 122). The arithmetic: ~16 billion cortical neurons (Azevedo 2009) in 66 days is about 170,000 a minute, against Cowan's whole-brain 250,000. The preplate, its splitting into marginal zone and subplate, the cortical plate from stage 21 (~Day 63), inside-out layering, and the finding that the radial glia guiding migration are the progenitors themselves — Rakic's radial unit made of cells. The first reflex: Hooker 1936 (Yale J Biol Med), a 25 mm fetus turning neck and trunk away from a hair drawn across the mouth, a spinal circuit a week or so from now, with his own caveats; why it differs from the spontaneous bends of Day 49, and why neither is a feeling. Then the one physical thing that can reach a tissue of dividing cells: ionising radiation. Otake & Schull's atomic-bomb reanalysis (1996): severe intellectual disability concentrated at 8–15 weeks after ovulation — Day 70 to Day 119, matching the factory's run; CDC/NCRP 174: 40% with IQ <70 after 1 Gy at 8–15 weeks, 15% at 16–25, non-cancer effects not detectable below 100 mGy; ACOG Committee Opinion 723: nothing associated with anomalies or loss below 50 mGy, intellectual disability only documented at ≥610 mGy. The doses: chest X-ray 0.0005–0.01 mGy, extremity <0.001, head CT 0.001–0.01, chest CT/CTPA 0.01–0.66, abdominal X-ray 0.1–3, lumbar spine 1–10, abdominal CT 1.3–35, pelvic CT 10–50 (≈2.5 low-dose), technetium scans <5; ten thousand chest films to the 100 mGy line; background ~1 mSv a year; a flight under 0.1 mSv (Day 32). The cancer side, which has no threshold: the Oxford Survey's leukaemia RR 1.49 (1.33–1.67) after ~6 mGy obstetric films; Wakeford & Little's 8% per Gy excess absolute childhood cancer risk on a baseline of ~1 in 630 — about 1 in 500 extra from a 25 mGy abdominal CT, about 1 in a million from a chest film. ACOG's rule: a needed scan is a needed scan; ultrasound and MRI first for the abdomen and pelvis; dental films safe (ACOG CO 569). And lead: Hu 2006 (146 Mexico City pairs; first-trimester lead predicted 24-month MDI, −3.5 points per SD plasma lead, later trimesters did not), the CDC 2010 risk-factor list for the first visit, the 5 µg/dL line, bone lead mobilised in pregnancy, and the sanding rule.
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, two lines in the pregnancy file. One: on the Day 40 question sheet, question fourteen in two parts — any X-rays or scans she has had since Day 14 (what and roughly when), and the lead risk list read out loud together (house age and any sanding, her work, imported food and glazed pottery, remedies and cosmetics, hobbies); if any item is a yes, write 'blood lead test?' beside it. Two: a card behind her insurance card that says 'I'm pregnant' with the due date, for whoever holds the X-ray button. If any renovation is planned before Day 280, write the rule on page one: she is out of the building for sanding or scraping, dust is contained and wet-wiped, and paint in a house older than 1978 is tested before it is touched.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 56 · Week 8 — Body: the week the body gets measured
item.description:
A raspberry growing a millimetre a day, the first bone, the gut that lives in the cord, and the one number that can move the due date.
Week 8 opens with the fifth Body episode. Your baby is at the turn from Carnegie stage 17 to 18 (11–17 mm; the NHS's 16 mm raspberry), growing close to a millimetre a day: pigmented eyes with eyelid folds beginning, the nasolacrimal groove, auricular hillocks merging into an ear, coronary arteries connecting to the aorta, a liver prominence, notches cutting between the finger rays, a thigh, an ankle and a foot plate, the lip fused. The first bone: the clavicle's shaft ossifies first, its two centres merging around post-fertilization day 45, with the femur (~day 43) and tibia (~day 44) behind it, and limb ossification starting at stage 18 (UNSW/Keibel & Mall). Physiological midgut herniation — the gut in the cord — in essentially every embryo at 10 weeks and 5% at 12 (Bogers 2019, 112 women, 699 scans), so the bump at the cord is normal. Why the NHS says 'fetus' at 8 weeks and this show says Day 70. Then the crown-rump length in full: Robinson & Fleming's 1975 Glasgow curve (±4.7 days), Hadlock 1992 (416 pregnancies, ±8%), INTERGROWTH-21st (4,607 women, 8 countries, SD ~2.4 days rising with length), ACOG Committee Opinion 700's ±5–7 days and its redating thresholds (>5 days before 9 weeks, >7 from 9 to 13+6), and the rule that the earliest good scan sets the date and later scans measure size, not age. What early scanning changes (Cochrane 2015: post-term induction RR 0.59 in 25,516 women; undetected twins RR 0.07; perinatal death RR 0.89, no difference). How often the measurement is taken wrong (Jakubowski 2020: 40% of 806 images rated accurate; neutral position the criterion that changes the date) and the one question to ask. The NHS 10–14-week scan and the 45–84 mm window. Tong 2008: 1.5% loss after a heartbeat at 8 weeks. And the first quantitative test of the thesis: in 1,631 Generation R pregnancies, smoking without folic acid cost 3.84 mm of crown-rump length by the dating scan, and the smallest fifth had 2.1× the odds of preterm birth, 2.4× low birth weight and 2.6× SGA (Mook-Kanamori 2010).
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight with the Day 42 index card. On the back write 'CRL ___ mm, measured on Day ___, due date ___'. Find out which scan sets the date (this week's first visit or a later dating scan) and write that date on the Day 40 question sheet; if no scan is booked before Day 98, add question thirteen: will we have a dating scan before 14 weeks, and if not, why. At the scan, fill the blanks and ask one question: was the baby in a neutral position for that? Then write underneath: 'This is the due date. Later scans measure size, not age.'
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 55 · Week 7 — Myths: lifting causes miscarriage, arms over her head wrap the cord round the neck, and she's eating for two
item.description:
The fourth Myths episode, closing Week 7. Your baby is 10–14.5 mm at Carnegie stage 17, ~41 days post-fertilization: definite finger rays, forward-facing nostrils, a full set of ear hillocks, a straightening trunk; the NHS grape on the way to next week's raspberry, inside a womb the size of a lemon. Myth one, lifting: 64% of 1,084 Americans believe it causes miscarriage and 76% blame stress (Bardos 2015); ACOG puts early loss at 10% of recognised pregnancies, 80% in the first trimester, ~50% chromosomal, with age and prior loss the named risk factors; the uterus is still inside the bony pelvis (Day 53). Thirty pooled studies: lifting >100 kg/day OR 1.32 (0.93–1.87), 1.02 in the better ones (Bonde 2013). The one real signal: 71,500 Danish working women, 2,830 fetal deaths — early miscarriage HR 1.38 at 101–200 kg/day, 2.02 above 1,000 kg/day, 2.74 (1.42–5.26) for >10 lifts of >20 kg a day, no stillbirth signal, and only 52 of 1,266 early losses recorded prospectively (Juhl 2013). Strain in the implantation window RR 2.5 (Hjollund 2000) — a window that closed on Day 23. Exercise: Madsen's HR 3.7 for >7 h/week, recalled after the loss, against Davenport's 46 studies and 266,778 women, miscarriage OR 0.88 (0.63–1.21). NIOSH-derived provisional occupational limits: 36 lb occasional / 18 lb repetitive before 20 weeks, 26 / 13 after (MacDonald & Waters 2013). Verdict: wrong for every lift at home; half right for an eight-hour lifting job, which is an employer conversation. Myth two, the cord: no guideline addresses it because no one has needed to; cord length is set by fetal movement pulling on it (Miller 1981), term length 50–60 cm; a nuchal cord is present in 12% at 24–26 weeks and 37% at term, wrapping and unwrapping (Clapp 2003), 33.7% of 11,748 term deliveries with no change in delivery or Apgar (Schäffer 2005), 14.7% of 166,318 deliveries with perinatal mortality 11 vs 16 per 1,000 (Sheiner 2006), 6.6% tight and 21.6% loose in 219,337 births with no clinically significant harm (Henry 2013), stillbirth OR 1.11 (0.62–1.98) across 145 studies (Hayes 2020), and entanglement in 20.7% of 856,300 Norwegian births driven by long cords, themselves predicted by maternal height, parity, BMI and diabetes (Linde 2018). The one true hazard of arms overhead is a first-trimester dizzy spell on a stepladder (Days 30, 44). Myth three, eating for two: the estimated energy requirement is +0 kcal/day in the first trimester, +340 in the second, +452 in the third (IOM DRI), and the measured cost is ~90, 290 and 470 kcal/day, ~77,000 kcal in total (Butte & King 2005); NICE: no need to eat for two, energy needs unchanged in the first six months, ~200 kcal/day in the last three; NHS: 'there's no need to eat for 2', even with twins. The embryo eats through the yolk sac and uterine glands (Day 51); what the trimester needs is folate, iodine, iron and fish, not calories. IOM…
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: on the Myths page of the pregnancy file, write this week's three answers in your own words, short enough for a family dinner — 'lifting's fine; it's an eight-hour-a-day lifting job that's the question'; 'the cord's length is the baby's doing, and a third of babies are born with it round their neck and do fine'; 'zero extra calories till Day 91, a sandwich a day after'. Two: weigh her once this week, same scale, in the morning, and write the number and date in the pregnancy file as the baseline the weight-gain band is measured from; then the scale goes under the bed until the first visit. If her job involves lifting more than 20 kg more than ten times a shift, add question twelve to the Day 40 sheet: lifting at work, and what the note to the employer should say.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

NIOSH-derived provisional occupational limits: 36 lb occasional / 18 lb repetitive before 20 weeks, 26 / 13 after (MacDonald & Waters 2013). Verdict: wrong for every lift at home; half right for an eight-hour lifting job, which is an employer conversation. Myth two, the cord: no guideline addresses it because no one has needed to; cord length is set by fetal movement pulling on it (Miller 1981), term length 50–60 cm; a nuchal cord is present in 12% at 24–26 weeks and 37% at term, wrapping and unwrapping (Clapp 2003), 33.7% of 11,748 term deliveries with no change in delivery or Apgar (Schäffer 2005), 14.7% of 166,318 deliveries with perinatal mortality 11 vs 16 per 1,000 (Sheiner 2006), 6.6% tight and 21.6% loose in 219,337 births with no clinically significant harm (Henry 2013), stillbirth OR 1.11 (0.62–1.98) across 145 studies (Hayes 2020), and entanglement in 20.7% of 856,300 Norwegian births driven by long cords, themselves predicted by maternal height, parity, BMI and diabetes (Linde 2018). The one true hazard of arms overhead is a first-trimester dizzy spell on a stepladder (Days 30, 44). Myth three, eating for two: the estimated energy requirement is +0 kcal/day in the first trimester, +340 in the second, +452 in the third (IOM DRI), and the measured cost is ~90, 290 and 470 kcal/day, ~77,000 kcal in total (Butte & King 2005); NICE: no need to eat for two, energy needs unchanged in the first six months, ~200 kcal/day in the last three; NHS: 'there's no need to eat for 2', even with twins. The embryo eats through the yolk sac and uterine glands (Day 51); what the trimester needs is folate, iodine, iron and fish, not calories. IOM…

Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: on the Myths page of the pregnancy file, write this week's three answers in your own words, short enough for a family dinner — 'lifting's fine; it's an eight-hour-a-day lifting job that's the question'; 'the cord's length is the baby's doing, and a third of babies are born with it round their neck and do fine'; 'zero extra calories till Day 91, a sandwich a day after'. Two: weigh her once this week, same scale, in the morning, and write the number and date in the pregnancy file as the baseline the weight-gain band is measured from; then the scale goes under the bed until the first visit. If her job involves lifting more than 20 kg more than ten times a shift, add question twelve to the Day 40 sheet: lifting at work, and what the note to the employer should say.

item.itunes:title: Day 55 · Week 7 — Myths: lifting causes miscarriage, arms over her head wrap the cord round the neck, and she's eating for two

item.title: Day 54 · Week 7 — Protocol: the medication audit
item.description:
Four piles from the cabinet photos, acetaminophen against the anti-inflammatories, the three prescriptions women stop that they shouldn't, the five that get switched this week, and the one-line rule to Day 280.
The fourth Protocol episode, built from the bathroom-cabinet photographs taken on Day 49. Your baby is 11–13 mm at the turn into Carnegie stage 17, finger rays appearing, in the peak sensitivity window for heart, limbs and face that closes around Day 70. The baseline nobody states: 1 baby in 33 has a birth defect before anyone takes anything (CDC). How little is known: 2 of the 54 drugs women most commonly take in the first trimester have good human data (Thorpe 2013); 97.7% of drugs approved 2000–2010 had undetermined risk, taking a mean 27 years to be rated (Adam 2011). How much is taken: 81.2% of 9,459 women in 18 countries used a medicine, 47.7% paracetamol (Lupattelli 2014); first-trimester prescription use up >60% in three decades (Mitchell 2011); 28.9% used herbals (Kennedy 2013). The letters A–X are gone (FDA PLLR, 2015); MotherToBaby (866-626-6847) and UK bumps replace them. Four piles. Pile two first: acetaminophen stays first-line (the 2.48-million-child sibling study, HR 0.98; the September 2025 FDA/ACOG exchange from Day 36); NSAIDs come off the shelf — FDA 2020 bars them from 20 weeks (oligohydramnios within 48 h, reversible in 3–6 days; 30 weeks for the ductus), and the first-trimester miscarriage fight laid out in full: Quebec aOR 2.43 (4,705 cases), Israel HR 1.10 (65,457 women), Kaiser HR 1.59 and 1.45 vs acetaminophen users (1,097 women). The exception: low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks for high-risk women (USPSTF 2021 Grade B; ASPRE 4.3% → 1.6%), as question eleven on the Day 40 sheet. Pile one: the three stopped that shouldn't be — antidepressants (relapse 68% vs 26%, HR 5.0, Cohen 2006; cardiac RR 1.06 adjusted in 949,504 pregnancies; PPHN 31 vs 21 per 10,000, aOR 1.10; ACOG CPG 5 against discontinuing for pregnancy alone), asthma inhalers (LBW RR 1.46, preterm 1.41, preeclampsia 1.54 across 1.6 million; preterm excess gone with active management, RR 1.07; 20% exacerbate, 6% hospitalised; NAEPP: safer treated; budesonide, albuterol), and levothyroxine, which goes up ~30% this week (requirement +47%, from week 5–8, Alexander 2004; untreated mothers' children −7 IQ points, 19% ≤85, Haddow 1999). The switch list: ACE inhibitors/ARBs (Cooper RR 2.71; Bateman adjusted 0.89; established later-pregnancy fetopathy), warfarin (major defects OR 3.86, miscarriage 42% vs 14%, embryopathy 0.6%, window from week 8 = Day 56), valproate, isotretinoin (iPLEDGE). The OTC shelf by fact sheet: loratadine and cetirizine fine; pseudoephedrine waits (gastroschisis OR 1.8, 4.2 with acetaminophen, null in 2009; baseline 1 in 2,564); dextromethorphan fine; calcium carbonate fine two hours from iron; bismuth subsalicylate out; topical tretinoin out despite reassuring small cohorts. Pile three: vitamin A >10,000 IU PR 4.8, 1 in 57 (Rothman 1995), retinol capsules go, kelp goes, herbals treated as…
Today's action: Fifteen minutes tonight with the Day 49 photographs and one sheet. Four headings — hers daily, hers as needed, supplements, mine — and every name with its dose. Then three marks: a tick beside acetaminophen, the prenatal and anything the fact sheets cleared; a circle beside every daily prescription and anything on the switch list (ACE inhibitors/ARBs, warfarin, valproate, isotretinoin), with the prescriber's name — those are tomorrow morning's calls, levothyroxine or warfarin first; a line through ibuprofen, naproxen, bismuth subsalicylate, any retinol capsule, the retinoid cream and kelp, which go into a bag in your drawer. Save MotherToBaby, 866-626-6847 (or medicinesinpregnancy.org in the UK), in both phones as 'can she take this'. File the sheet behind the Day 40 question list and add question eleven: is she a low-dose aspirin candidate from 12 weeks?
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 53 · Week 7 — Adventure: the long drive
item.description:
The belt that halves fetal loss, the one woman in five who wears it right, the forty-two percent, and the clot in the passenger seat.
The fourth Adventure episode: the drive to her parents, the coast, the move. Your baby is 10–12 mm at the end of Carnegie stage 16, two days from finger rays — inside a uterus that is still inside the bony pelvis until about 12 weeks, so this trimester the car's risk to the pregnancy runs through its risk to her. The baseline: 39,345 US road deaths in 2024, 1.20 per 100 million vehicle miles (NHTSA), about one in 80,000 per thousand miles. How often pregnant women crash: 2.8% of 322,704 Utah pregnancies (Hyde 2003) and 2.9% of 878,546 North Carolina pregnancies, 12.6 per 1,000, 45% at 20–27 weeks, 1% unbelted (Vladutiu 2013). The surprise: crashes as a driver up 42% (95% CI 32–53) in the second trimester, 177 → 252 a month, in 507,262 Ontario women compared with themselves, not as passengers or pedestrians, gone by the third trimester (Redelmeier 2014) — so this trimester, you drive. What a crash does: 3.7 traumatic fetal deaths per 100,000 live births, 82% from crashes, placental injury in 42% (Weiss 2001); belted women in crashes indistinguishable from women never in a crash, unbelted women 2.8× the fetal deaths, 1.3× low birthweight, 2× serious bleeding (Hyde 2003); preterm birth +23%, abruption +34%, PROM +32% after one crash, stillbirth ×4.8 after two, unbelted stillbirth ×2.77 (Vladutiu 2013); proper belt use OR 4.5 for an acceptable fetal outcome and about half of crash fetal losses preventable (Klinich 2008, 57 investigated crashes); belts prevent brain, chest and pelvic injury with no added risk to pregnant occupants in 1998–2021 federal crash data (Espelien 2025). Who wears it: 88.5% of pregnant vs 88.8% of non-pregnant women 'always', flat trend vs rising for everyone else, in 1.39 million BRFSS respondents (Espelien 2023); only 21% of 824 pregnant women position both belts correctly vs 39% (Kidd 2025). The NHTSA placement: lap belt under the belly on the hips, shoulder belt between the breasts, never under the arm or behind the back, no slack, upright, as far from the wheel as possible (≈10 in / 25 cm), airbags on (SOGC: no evidence to disable; Metz 2006: 1 abruption in 30 deployments), no aftermarket adjusters, any crash assessed the same day. The clot: travel of any mode RR 2.8, +18% per 2 hours (Chandra 2009) on the Day 32 pregnancy baseline; NHS stockings over 4 hours, movement every 30 minutes, water, share the driving; HealthLink BC ≤4 hours' driving a day, a stop every 2 hours. Drowsy driving: 66,000–90,000 police-reported crashes and ~800 deaths a year, undercounted (NHTSA 2017), against Day 30's 44% daily fatigue. Nausea, heat and the Day 46 hospital list reapplied; the verdict: the trip is on, the kid comes along.
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, in the car, with her. Passenger seat first: slide it all the way back, sit her in it, and set the belt together — lap belt under the belly and across the hips, shoulder belt between the breasts and off the neck, slack out. Driver's seat: she adjusts it to reach the pedals with ten inches (a hand-span and a half) between breastbone and wheel, and it stays there. Say the three nevers once each: never over the bump, never under the arm, never behind the back. Then the rule for the next drive, typed into both phones under the Day 51 bleeding rule: you drive the long legs; a stop every two hours; flight socks if any leg is over four; the Day 39 bottle in the cup holder; any bump, at any speed, is a same-day call to the practice. If there is a maternity belt adjuster in the house, it goes in the bin.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 52 · Week 7 — Parents: when to tell people
item.description:
The twelve-week rule against the evidence, the one woman in nine who has been there, the workplace numbers, and the first shot of the pregnancy, which is also yours.
The fourth Parents episode. Your baby is 9–11 mm at Carnegie stage 16: dark eyes, a wrist, finger rays three days away. The twelve-week rule, taken apart: it is arithmetically right about the loss curve (a quarter of hormone-detected conceptions gone before 6 weeks, Wilcox 1999; 10% at age 25–29, Magnus 2019; ~4% after a heartbeat at 7 weeks, Tong 2008) and socially backwards about what people are for. What people believe (Bardos 2015, n = 1,084): 55% think miscarriage happens in ≤5% of pregnancies, 76% blame stress, 64% lifting; of those who had one, 47% felt guilty, 41% alone, 28% ashamed, and 28% felt less isolated when a public figure spoke. What is true (Quenby, Lancet 2021): 15.3% of recognised pregnancies, 23 million a year, and 10.8% of women have had one — one in nine. What a loss does (Farren 2020, 737 women): PTSD criteria in 29% at one month and 18% at nine, anxiety 24% → 17%, depression 11% → 6%; partners (Farren 2021, 192 couples): 7%, 6% and 2% at one month, 4%, 6% and 1% at nine. What support does: low support and antenatal depression AOR 1.18 and anxiety 1.97 after correcting publication bias (Bedaso 2021, 64,449 women); miscarriage and low support compounding rather than adding for later depression in 179,000 UK Biobank women (Hu 2024); support programmes not changing birth weight or preterm birth (Cochrane 2019, 25 trials). The early list and the scan list, and whose decision it is. Work: 77% of UK mothers with a negative or discriminatory experience and 11% dismissed, made redundant or forced out (~54,000 a year); the US Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (June 2023, 15+ employees, accommodations once the limitation is communicated, no note for common needs, no retaliation); UK notice at 15 weeks before the expected week of childbirth, with protections starting when the employer knows. Then the flu shot: 5% of 2009 pandemic deaths from the ~1% of the population that was pregnant, 22.6% of hospitalised women to ICU, treatment after day 4 carrying 6× the ICU risk (Siston 2010); nearly half of hospitalised women aged 15–49 pregnant in autumn 2022 (CDC); 40% protection against flu hospitalisation across 2 million pregnancies (Thompson 2019); 63% fewer confirmed infant infections in Bangladesh (Zaman 2008, 340 mothers) and 50.4%/48.8% maternal/infant efficacy in South Africa (Madhi 2014, 2,116 women); the miscarriage signal (Donahue 2017, aOR 2.0, 7.7 in repeat vaccinees) and the prospective null that followed (Donahue 2019, aOR 0.9, 1,236 cases); Cochrane's healthy-adult numbers for the father (2.3% → 0.9%, NNV 71); ACIP 2025–26 (inactivated, any trimester, September–October preferred for the first and second trimester, single-dose thimerosal-free, no nasal spray) and the NHS (all pregnant women, any stage, from September).
Today's action: Fifteen minutes tonight, one sheet, two columns. Left: the people you would both want to already know if it went wrong — the ones who would just show up; she decides every name and you say which of them are yours. Right: everyone else, with the scan date from the Day 42 card as the default. The first row of the left column gets told this week, in her words. Underneath: her flu shot booked for this week if the season is open where you live (inactivated, not the spray), and yours booked for the same day at the same pharmacy; if the season isn't open yet, the month it opens goes in your calendar now.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 51 · Week 7 — Physiology: the organ she's growing for someone else
item.description:
How a grape-sized embryo eats with no blood supply, the plugs that keep the oxygen out until Day 70, the hormone handover, and what spotting means.
The fourth Physiology episode, and the placenta's. Your baby is 8–11 mm at Carnegie stage 16, dark-eyed, with a wrist forming; the placenta around it is many times its size and runs ahead of it all trimester. What it is (Burton & Jauniaux 2015: the fetus's lungs, gut, kidneys and liver plus a gland; ~500 g and 12–14 m² of villi at term). The discovery that the seven-week placenta is sealed from the mother's arteries: Hustin & Schaaps 1987 found no intervillous blood flow before 12 weeks in 250 scans, 70 specimens and 3 hysterectomies; electrodes measured placental oxygen under 20 mmHg at 8–10 weeks rising past 50 at 12 (Rodesch 1992; Jauniaux 2000, 2001) — a fifth of adult tissue, by design, to protect organogenesis from free radicals (Burton 2009). What the embryo eats instead: uterine gland secretions, active to week 10, swallowed by the placenta and filtered to the yolk sac, which feeds the gut (Burton 2002; Hempstock 2004; Jauniaux & Gulbis 2000). The valve opening around Day 70, the oxidative burst the placenta prepares for, and the spiral-artery conversion — half a millimetre to 2.5 mm, 2–3 m/s to 10 cm/s — whose failure underlies early pre-eclampsia and growth restriction (Pijnenborg 2006; Burton 2009), and whose premature failure is the common mechanism of miscarriage (Jauniaux, Poston & Burton 2006). The hormone handover from the Day 30 corpus luteum: hCG's jobs (Cole 2010), its peak and 18-week nadir in 443 women (Braunstein 1976), placental GDF15 as the sickness curve (Fejzo 2024), and progesterone and placental lactogen rewiring her appetite (Burton & Fowden 2015). Then spotting: Hasan 2009's 27% from Day 38, and the subchorionic haematoma — one extra loss in 11 in the older bleeding-based literature (Tuuli 2011, 1,735 women) versus no independent association in 2,446 routinely scanned pregnancies once dates and bleeding are adjusted for (Naert 2019, 18.4% prevalence) — with the NHS/ACOG bleeding rule in one line.
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: on the Day 42 index card, add two dates — Day 70, 'the valve opens: maternal blood reaches the placenta, oxygen starts to climb', and Day 84, 'placenta fully running; organ-building done, growth begins'. Two: type the bleeding rule into both phones under the Day 28 after-hours number: any bleeding, call the practice or early pregnancy unit today; severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness, or a pad soaked in an hour, emergency care now. If she has already had spotting this week and hasn't called, make the call together tomorrow morning.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

The fourth Physiology episode, and the placenta's. Your baby is 8–11 mm at Carnegie stage 16, dark-eyed, with a wrist forming; the placenta around it is many times its size and runs ahead of it all trimester. What it is (Burton & Jauniaux 2015: the fetus's lungs, gut, kidneys and liver plus a gland; ~500 g and 12–14 m² of villi at term). The discovery that the seven-week placenta is sealed from the mother's arteries: Hustin & Schaaps 1987 found no intervillous blood flow before 12 weeks in 250 scans, 70 specimens and 3 hysterectomies; electrodes measured placental oxygen under 20 mmHg at 8–10 weeks rising past 50 at 12 (Rodesch 1992; Jauniaux 2000, 2001) — a fifth of adult tissue, by design, to protect organogenesis from free radicals (Burton 2009). What the embryo eats instead: uterine gland secretions, active to week 10, swallowed by the placenta and filtered to the yolk sac, which feeds the gut (Burton 2002; Hempstock 2004; Jauniaux & Gulbis 2000). The valve opening around Day 70, the oxidative burst the placenta prepares for, and the spiral-artery conversion — half a millimetre to 2.5 mm, 2–3 m/s to 10 cm/s — whose failure underlies early pre-eclampsia and growth restriction (Pijnenborg 2006; Burton 2009), and whose premature failure is the common mechanism of miscarriage (Jauniaux, Poston & Burton 2006). The hormone handover from the Day 30 corpus luteum: hCG's jobs (Cole 2010), its peak and 18-week nadir in 443 women (Braunstein 1976), placental GDF15 as the sickness curve (Fejzo 2024), and progesterone and placental lactogen rewiring her appetite (Burton & Fowden 2015). Then spotting: Hasan 2009's 27% from Day 38, and the subchorionic haematoma — one extra loss in 11 in the older bleeding-based literature (Tuuli 2011, 1,735 women) versus no independent association in 2,446 routinely scanned pregnancies once dates and bleeding are adjusted for (Naert 2019, 18.4% prevalence) — with the NHS/ACOG bleeding rule in one line.

Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: on the Day 42 index card, add two dates — Day 70, 'the valve opens: maternal blood reaches the placenta, oxygen starts to climb', and Day 84, 'placenta fully running; organ-building done, growth begins'. Two: type the bleeding rule into both phones under the Day 28 after-hours number: any bleeding, call the practice or early pregnancy unit today; severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness, or a pad soaked in an hour, emergency care now. If she has already had spotting this week and hasn't called, make the call together tomorrow morning.

The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.itunes:title: Day 51 · Week 7 — Physiology: the organ she's growing for someone else

item.title: Day 50 · Week 7 — Brain: three bubbles become five
item.description:
The hemispheres bud, the cerebellum starts a three-year build, the first cortex is ten days away, and the one brain nutrient we hadn't covered.
The fourth Brain episode, on the last day of the thalidomide limb window. Your baby is 8–11 mm at the turn from Carnegie stage 15 to 16 (NHS: a grape, with a forehead; about 100 new brain cells a minute). O'Rahilly & Müller's 192-embryo series: the five chief brain subdivisions are recognisable this week — hemispheres budding from the telencephalon, thalamus and hypothalamus, midbrain, pons-and-cerebellum, medulla — and the cortical plate does not appear until stage 21 (~Day 63). The cerebellum's four-step, three-year build (ten Donkelaar 2003), why it is the structure most damaged by prematurity (Volpe 2009), and its 34-fold growth in the second half of pregnancy alone (Andescavage 2017, 166 fetuses). The growth curve: ~350–400 g at birth, quadrupling by three (Dekaban 1978, 4,736 brains); 86 billion neurons counted, not 100 billion, with 19% in the cortex and ~80% in the cerebellum (Azevedo 2009); 100 a minute now against ~250,000 a minute averaged over gestation (Cowan 1979). Rakic's radial units and the extra rounds of division that separate a mouse cortex from a human one; synaptogenesis before 27 weeks, peaks at 3 and 15 months, pruning into adolescence (Huttenlocher 1997); the Harvard Center's million connections a second after birth. Then what her blood carries to it this week — not much blood, by design — and the nutrient the show hadn't covered: iron. Georgieff 2020; 35.5% of pregnant women anaemic worldwide (WHO 2023); US iron deficiency 7% → 14% → 30% by trimester (Mei 2011); cord ferritin and five-year outcomes in 278 children (Tamura 2002); 532,232 Swedish children, early maternal anaemia and autism OR 1.44, ADHD 1.37, intellectual disability 2.20, holding within families (Wiegersma 2019); 44 trials, 43,274 women, anaemia at term −70% (Cochrane 2015); ACOG PB 233's first-visit blood count. And the father's one finished contribution: ~2 new mutations per year of paternal age (Kong 2012), autism RR 1.66 for fathers ≥50 in 5.77 million children (Sandin 2016), schizophrenia doubled over 45 (Malaspina 2001) — real, modest, and nothing to do.
Today's action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: add question ten to the Day 40 sheet — is a full blood count in today's bloods, can a ferritin go with it, and what are her two numbers (not just 'normal')? Write them in the pregnancy file with the date when they come back. Two: check the iron line on the Day 33 label photo (~27 mg), cook one iron meal this week (red meat, or lentils and beans, with something vitamin-C rich on the plate), and move her tea or coffee at least an hour away from the vitamin. If she is vegetarian or vegan, or has had anaemia or heavy periods before, add to question ten: should she start extra iron now?
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 49 · Week 7 — Body: the week the body gets its edges
item.description:
Fingers from a paddle, a lip from three pieces, a wall down the heart, the calendar a drug disaster wrote, and the first movement nobody feels.
Week 7 opens with the fourth Body episode. Your baby is 8–10 mm (the NHS's grape) at the end of Carnegie stage 15: the arm bud split into hand plate and arm, the hand plate about to divide into wrist and digital plate, digital rays by ~Day 55 and free fingers by ~Day 63; a lip assembling from three pieces (CDC: weeks 4–7) and a palate behind it (weeks 6–9); nasal pits turning forward, dark eyes, auricular hillocks; a foramen secundum opening in the upper heart by design while the lower wall grows and the outflow divides, walled off by ~Day 63 and finished by ~Day 70. Why we know the schedule to the day: thalidomide, sold from 1957 for sedation and morning sickness, damaged more than 10,000 children, and Lenz's reconstruction from prescription dates gave a calendar in LMP days — no defects before Day 34 or after Day 50; absent ears Days 35–37, absent arms 39–41, phocomelia with three fingers 43–44, three-jointed thumbs 46–48 — so the limb window closes tomorrow. The three edges with their numbers: the lip (1 in 1,031 cleft lip ± palate; folic acid ≥400 µg aOR 0.61 in 377 Norwegian cases, Wilcox 2007; smoking RR 1.34 across 24 studies, Little 2004; first-trimester fever 1.5–3×, Dreier 2014); the heart (9.1 per 1,000 worldwide across 24 million births, van der Linde 2011; ~40,000 US babies a year, 1 in 4 critical, CDC; pregestational diabetes RR 4.0 — 318 vs 80 per 10,000 — in 2 million Danes, Øyen 2016; NBDPS aOR 3.17 isolated and 8.62 multiple defects, Correa 2008; severe CHD falling 6% a year after flour fortification in 1.3 million Quebec births, Ionescu-Ittu 2009); and the limbs, which after thalidomide are about drugs that cross, handled by the Day 54 audit. The first movement: a one-second sideways bend of head or rump at 7 weeks in 18 IVF embryos (Lüchinger 2008), limbs joining by 8.5 weeks, whole-body general movements at 9–10 weeks, never still more than 13 minutes between 8 and 19 weeks (de Vries 1982, 1985), felt by the mother only at ~16–22 weeks. Scan numbers if it is this week: mean heart rate 125 at Days 46–49 and 145 at 50–52 (Stefos 1998); miscarriage 4.2% after a heartbeat at 7 completed weeks (Tong 2008). The point: the schedule is daily, the list of what can reach it is the same list since Day 29, and the father's job is maintenance, not vigilance.
Today's action: Tonight, ten minutes, in the pregnancy file. Write three dates and what closes on each: Day 56, the lip is fused and the finger rays are drawn; Day 63, the fingers are free and the lower heart is walled off; Day 70, the palate, and the end of organ-building. Under them, four lines already running: folic acid 400 µg every morning; no smoke in the house, hers or yours; over 38 °C (100.4 °F) is acetaminophen and a call; nothing new from a pharmacy, health-food shop or friend's cabinet without the call, and nothing she already takes stopped without it. Then photograph every packet, bottle and tube in the bathroom cabinet, hers and yours, so the Day 54 medication audit starts from a picture. If your partner has diabetes, add one line: her last A1c and when the next one is.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 48 · Week 6 — Myths: get rid of the cat, put down the hair dye, and stay out of the hot bath
item.description:
The third Myths episode, on the last day of Week 6, and the day the Day 36 promise on hot tubs is paid. Your baby is 7–9 mm at Carnegie stage 15: lens vesicles sealed and going dark with pigment, nasal pits, hand plates, the foramen secundum opening in the upper heart by design, the first gut loop, lobar lung buds and the hemispheres marked out. Myth one, 'get rid of the cat': wrong about the animal, right about the parasite. 91% of US women are susceptible, and the two case-control studies on how pregnant women actually get infected agree — undercooked lamb, beef and game, soil and travel in six European cities (Cook 2000: 'contact with cats was not a risk factor'; 30–63% of infections from meat, 6–17% from soil), and in the US rare lamb aOR 8.4, raw ground beef 6.7, cured meat 2.0, with the one cat finding being three or more kittens at aOR 27.9 (Jones 2009). Why: a cat sheds oocysts for about one week in its life and never again on rechallenge (Davis & Dubey 1995), and oocysts are not infectious until 1–5 days after shedding (CDC), which a daily litter change beats. Myth two, 'no hair dye': mostly a myth. The NHS says most research shows it is safe and 12 weeks is a choice, not a rule; 0.5% of a labelled dark permanent dye was absorbed in eight volunteers (Hueber-Becker 2004); no signal for preterm birth or low birth weight with harsher straighteners (Blackmore-Prince 1999, 525 women); Motherisk calls 3–4 uses a pregnancy not of concern; one positive study for neuroblastoma (McCall 2005, OR 1.6 on a baseline of ~8 per million children a year) against null findings for childhood brain tumours (Holly 2002, 540 cases) and leukaemia (Towle 2017, 20 studies, meta-RR 1.09). Myth three, 'no hot baths': half right. Heat is a teratogen with a 39.0 °C threshold; hot tubs carried RR 2.8 for neural tube defects in 23,491 women (Milunsky 1992), hyperthermia OR 1.92 across 15 studies (Moretti 2005), anencephaly aOR 1.68 and gastroschisis 1.54 in the NBDPS with ≥2-fold odds for long repeated use (Duong 2011), and a possible doubling of miscarriage in 1,063 Kaiser women (Li 2003). But it takes ≥15 min to the neck at 39 °C or ≥10 min at 41 °C to approach the threshold (Harvey 1981), a 40 °C bath leaves pregnant women at a mean 36.9 °C and a 70 °C sauna at 37.6 °C (Ravanelli 2019, 347 women, 20-minute limits), and 98.5% of Finnish mothers use the sauna in pregnancy with one of the lowest CNS-defect rates ever recorded (Saxén 1982). The neural tube sealed around Day 42; the heart and face are still closing. Verdict: bath yes, sauna at 70 °C for 20 minutes yes, hot tub 10 minutes with shoulders out or skip until 12 weeks.
Today's action: Tonight, two things, ten minutes. One: the litter tray is yours until the birth — say it out loud, put it on the chore list, do it daily with a hand wash after (gloves if you like); if there is a kitten, a raw-fed cat or a cat that hunts, the garden gloves go next to it. Two: put a cheap baby bath thermometer in the bathroom and tell her the two numbers: 40 °C (104 °F) is a bath she can stay in; a hot tub is ten minutes with her shoulders out until twelve weeks. If she's been holding off on colouring her hair, tell her what the NHS says and book it.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 47 · Week 6 — Protocol: the kitchen rules
item.description:
One bacterium, one metal, one parasite, the fish list that says eat more, and the thermometer that settles most of it.
The third Protocol episode, for the father who took over the kitchen on Day 37. Your baby is 5–7 mm at the turn to Carnegie stage 15, lens vesicles closing, nasal pits, hand plates, and a gut that is a straight tube feeding on nothing — so only what crosses her blood matters. One bacterium justifies the list: Listeria, ~1,250 US cases and 172 deaths a year, about 1 pregnant woman in 25,000, 1 in 4 of them losing the pregnancy or newborn (CDC); in the French MONALISA cohort (818 cases, 107 maternal-neonatal) only 5% of pregnancies were uneventful, 24% ended in fetal loss, and no loss occurred after 29 weeks or more than 2 days after admission — early treatment works. The 2003 FDA/FSIS risk assessment by food: deli meats ~77 cases per billion servings and the majority of all cases, unreheated frankfurters 65, smoked seafood 6, soft unripened cheese 2, pasteurised milk 1, a reheated frankfurter 0.06; the 2011 cantaloupe outbreak (147 ill, 33 dead, 7 pregnancy-related, 1 miscarriage) and the 2024 deli-slicer outbreak (61 hospitalised, 10 dead). The CDC and NHS swap lists, and the size: roughly one in a million sandwiches, fixed by 165 °F. One metal justifies a short list: the FDA/EPA advice is 8–12 oz of fish a week, 2–3 servings, with seven species to avoid, and the FDA table shows why — swordfish 0.995 ppm, shark 0.979, bigeye 0.689, albacore 0.35, light tuna 0.126, salmon 0.022, scallops 0.003; ALSPAC's 11,875 mothers (Hibbeln 2007): no seafood, verbal-IQ bottom quartile OR 1.48. One parasite justifies a thermometer: Toxoplasma, 91% of US women susceptible (NHANES), transmission 6% at 13 weeks to 72% at 36 (Dunn 1999, 603 infections), 30–63% of infections from undercooked or cured meat and cats not a risk factor (Cook 2000); rare lamb aOR 8.4, raw ground beef 6.7, local cured meat 2.0 (Jones 2009); 2 congenital cases in 521,655 Californian births. USDA temperatures (145/160/165 °F), the ordinary bugs that don't cross (eggs, sprouts, raw juice, 40 °F, two hours), the three-agency sushi argument, the cross-references (liver, game, caffeine, alcohol), the fever-plus-aches rule, and the six-line fridge card.
Today's action: Tonight, three objects and one card. Buy a fridge thermometer and a probe thermometer tomorrow if they aren't in the house; tonight check the fridge is at or below 40 °F (4 °C). Move everything from the chilled ready-to-eat shelf — deli meat, hot dogs, soft cheese without 'pasteurised' on the label, smoked salmon, the tub of coleslaw, sprouts — to one shelf labelled 'heat or yours'. Write six lines on a card for the fridge door: ready-to-eat from the chiller gets heated to 165 °F; whole meat 145 °F and rest, ground 160, poultry 165; fish two to three times a week, not the seven big ones, tuna steak once; eggs firm or Lion; no sprouts, raw juice, raw milk or raw fish; fever plus aches is a call. Photograph the card for her phone.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 46 · Week 6 — Adventure: going up
item.description:
Altitude in the first trimester, the five studies that exist, the sleeping-altitude rule, and the one pill she shouldn't take.
The third Adventure episode: the ski week, the mountain town, the high city. Your baby is 5–7 mm at Carnegie stage 14, lens pits closing into vesicles — and already living at 'altitude': placental oxygen under 20 mmHg at 8 weeks, by design (Jauniaux 2000; Rodesch 1992; Eastman's 'Mount Everest in utero', 1954). The entire literature on pregnant altitude visitors is five small third-trimester studies and one survey (McManis 2021): a cable car to 2,228 m (transcutaneous PO2 71 → 58 mmHg, fetal heart rate 138 → 142, one smoker's fetus briefly slow), a chamber, ten commercial flights, seven women exercising to maximum at 6,000 ft (fetal heart rate unchanged; Artal 1995), and one Sherpa guide at 5,300 m — reassuring, and not one first-trimester woman among them. The resident data that people will quote: birthweight −102 g per 1,000 m in 3,836 Colorado births (Jensen & Moore 1997), pre-eclampsia 16% vs 3% at 3,100 m (Palmer 1999), growth restriction 16.8% vs 5.9% at 3,600 m in Bolivia (Keyes 2003) — nine months of placental work after 20 weeks, which is where every guideline draws its hard line. The real hazard is acute mountain sickness: 25% of 3,158 Colorado visitors, 65% within 12 hours, 3.5× for sea-level residents (Honigman 1993; CDC Yellow Book), with symptoms identical to Week 6 — so her PUQE score from Day 41 is the baseline. Acetazolamide: contraindicated in the first trimester by the UIAA on animal data; 50 human first-trimester exposures without a signal (Falardeau 2013) — reassuring, thin, and not for a holiday. The ascent profile from the Yellow Book (no first night above 2,750 m from low ground; 2–3 nights at 2,450–2,750; ≤500 m/day above 3,000; easy for 48 h) and the ceilings that agree: 2,500 m for short stays (UIAA; Huch 1996), 1,800–2,500 m for acclimatised moderate exercise (ACOG CO 804; Mottola 2018), 'prudent' not to sleep above 3,050 m (CDC). Falls, dry air, and the one risk Week 6 adds: distance to a transvaginal probe. Three worked trips and the bed-not-summit rule.
Today's action: Tonight, ten minutes, with the next mountain trip open: write down the sleeping altitude for every night — the bed, not the lift-top. If any night is above 2,750 m and you arrive from low ground, add a night at 2,400–2,750 m on the way up; if any night is above 3,050 m, move it lower or move the trip, and make that the OB question this week. Find the nearest hospital with obstetric ultrasound to where you'll sleep, with the drive time, and save it in both phones under the Day 28 after-hours number. Put the Day 39 bottle and the PUQE score on the packing list. No acetazolamide this pregnancy — the ascent profile replaces it.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 45 · Week 6 — Parents: your head
item.description:
The father nobody screens, the hormone that is already falling, and the treatment with a thousand trials behind it.
The third Parents episode, and the one about the father. Your baby is 5–7 mm at the start of Carnegie stage 14: lens pits sinking into the sides of the head, arm buds lengthening, the brain half again as large as yesterday. The shape of the thing: in 312 first-time fathers followed from 23 weeks to one year, symptom levels were highest in pregnancy (Condon 2004); stress peaks at the birth, driven by role restriction and being an onlooker (Philpott 2017). The numbers: paternal depression 8.4% across 74 studies and 41,480 men (Cameron 2016), 13.6% in the first trimester (Rao 2020), 10.4% overall (Paulson & Bazemore 2010); paternal anxiety 4.1–16% in pregnancy and 2.4–18% postnatally (Leach 2016) against 18.2% first-trimester anxiety symptoms in mothers (Dennis 2017); a preconception history of major depression carrying 6× the odds of perinatal depression and 4× of anxiety (Lowrie 2022); resident fathers' depressive symptoms rising 68% across the first five years of fatherhood in 10,623 men (Garfield 2014). The body: testosterone falling a median 26% (waking) and 34% (evening) in 624 men who became fathers, lowest in those doing 3+ hours of daily care (Gettler 2011); significant declines in testosterone and estradiol across pregnancy in 29 expectant fathers (Edelstein 2015); low testosterone going with paternal depression but high testosterone with maternal depression, aggression and fathering stress in 149 couples (Saxbe 2017) — so don't 'fix' it; BMI drifting up with fatherhood (Garfield 2016); sleep down 13 minutes for men versus 62 for women, unrecovered at six years (Richter 2019). The gap: ACOG CO 757 screens her, not you; fathers feel like bystanders across 22 qualitative studies (Baldwin 2018). The tools: the EPDS with a men's cut-off of 5/6 (Matthey 2001, 208 fathers) and the GAD-7 at 10 (Spitzer 2006; sensitivity 89%, specificity 82%). What works: father-specific trials are thin (11 studies; Rominov 2016); counselling cuts perinatal depression onset 39% in at-risk pregnant women (O'Connor 2019, USPSTF) and psychosocial support cuts postpartum depression 22% (Cochrane 2013); and physical activity, in 97 reviews, 1,039 trials and 128,119 people, has medium effects on depression (−0.43), anxiety (−0.42) and distress (−0.60), larger at higher intensity (Singh 2023), with Cochrane's exercise-for-depression review agreeing. Showing up is, on this evidence, also what helps you.
Today's action: Tonight, fifteen minutes, alone first: find the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and the GAD-7, take both, and write the two numbers and the date in the pregnancy file under your partner's entry from the Day 40 sheet. Six or more on the Edinburgh (the men's cut-off) or ten or more on the GAD-7 means you book an appointment with your own doctor this week and say 'my partner's six weeks pregnant and I scored above the line on a screen.' If you have had a depression before, book it anyway. Either way, put three thirty-minute exercise sessions in your own calendar for the next seven days and make one of them her walk. Then tell one person — your partner or a friend — the number you got.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 44 · Week 6 — Physiology: her heart is already running faster
item.description:
The pump, the blood, the breath, the heart-rate limit retired in 1994, and the real size of two hundred milligrams.
The third Physiology episode, promised on Day 43. Your baby is 4–6 mm at the end of Carnegie stage 13 (NHS: a pea), the heart looped and dividing; stage 14 and the lens pits begin tomorrow. Her cardiovascular rebuild happened before anything showed: heart rate up from 2–5 weeks (Hunter & Robson 1992; +8 bpm by 8 weeks in Clapp 1985), cardiac output significantly higher by 5 weeks LMP and 4.88 → 7.21 L/min by 32 weeks in 13 women (Robson 1989), +1 L/min by 8 weeks and vascular resistance at 70% of baseline (Capeless & Clapp 1989), a +31% peak in the early third trimester pooled over 39 studies (Meah 2016), plasma volume +50% (Pritchard 1965; Soma-Pillay 2016), and the reference curves from 36,000 women — systolic lowest at 10 weeks (110), diastolic at 21 weeks (66), heart rate 79 → 87 (Loerup 2019) — which explain the dizziness. The breath: minute ventilation up to +48% from the first trimester via tidal volume, PaCO2 ~30 mmHg, oxygen consumption +20%, breathlessness in ~70% of healthy pregnant women (LoMauro & Aliverti 2015). Then the heart-rate myth: ACOG's 1985 ceiling of 140 bpm and 15 minutes, withdrawn in 1994, still given by 62% of surveyed obstetricians in 2006 and invoked in 69% of discussions in 2005 (Entin & Munhall 2006; Krans 2005); what replaced it — ≥150 min/week she can talk through (ACOG CO 804; Mottola 2018) — and the evidence under it: GDM −38%, gestational hypertension −39%, pre-eclampsia −41% in RCTs of 273,182 women (Davenport 2018), miscarriage OR 0.88 and perinatal death OR 0.86 in 266,778 women (Davenport 2019), reassuring fetal Dopplers after peak treadmill tests (Szymanski & Satin 2012), the Day 39 heat limits, and the real exclusions. Then caffeine: half-life 3.4 → 8.3 h in pregnancy and 10.5 h near term (Knutti 1981/82), what is actually in the cup (FDA 113–247 mg per 12 oz brewed; NHS 100/75/40/80), the 200 mg ceiling (ACOG CO 462; NHS), the one RCT (1,197 women, −182 mg/day, no effect: Cochrane 2015), Weng 2008's aHR 2.23 at ≥200 mg against Savitz 2008's null with visible recall bias, Chen 2016's dose-response (RR 1.02 at 50–149 mg, 1.40 at 350–699, 1.72 at ≥700; +7% per 100 mg; 130,456 women), the nausea confounder, CARE 2008's growth-restriction trend (OR 1.5 at 200–299 mg; 2,635 women), and Hinkle 2021's reminder that 41% of American women drink none and under 1% exceed 200.
Today's action: Tonight, the caffeine audit, ten minutes: list everything with caffeine your partner had today and put a number beside each (instant ~100 mg a mug; coffee-shop coffee 150–300, look it up by brand and size; tea 75; cola 40; energy drink 80; dark chocolate 25). If the total is over 200 mg, she picks which one goes and you make it happen — buy decaf tomorrow for the second cup. If under, write the number on a card by the kettle so it stays under when the sickness lifts. Then one sentence to her about the stairs: it's the hormone, not her. And if anyone quotes 140 bpm, the answer is 'that was withdrawn in 1994; the rule is that she can talk.'
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 43 · Week 6 — Brain: the hormone she lends the brain
item.description:
Thyroxine, iodine, two big trials that didn't move an IQ, and the one line on the label.
The third Brain episode, picking up the line Day 36 ended on. Your baby is 4–6 mm at Carnegie stage 13; by stage 14 (~Day 45) the brain is about 50% larger, the velum transversum marks off the future cerebral hemispheres, the cerebellum begins as a thickening in rhombomere 1, the adenohypophysial pouch (future pituitary) is prominent, the first precocious neurons in the cord already send rootlets to muscle, and the thyroid is migrating down the neck but won't make hormone until ~Day 84 — so until then every molecule of thyroxine in the brain is hers (Morreale de Escobar 2004). Proof it crosses: cord thyroxine at a quarter to half of normal in newborns with no thyroid (Vulsma 1989). What the loan costs her: in 20 pregnancies on levothyroxine the requirement rose from week 5, median onset week 8, by a mean 47%, plateauing at week 16 (Alexander 2004) — a woman on levothyroxine raises her dose at the positive test (ACOG PB 223: ~25%). The cohorts: 7 IQ points lower in children of 48 untreated hypothyroid mothers, 19% vs 5% with IQ ≤85 (Haddow 1999, 25,216 sera); lower psychomotor scores at 10 months with lowest-decile free T4 at 12 weeks (Pop 1999, 220 women); an inverted U in 3,839 Generation R pairs — both low and high maternal free T4 at 9–18 weeks go with 1.4–3.8 fewer IQ points and less grey matter and cortex on 646 MRIs, while TSH predicts nothing (Korevaar 2016). The trials: CATS screened 21,846 women at 12w3d and treated 390 from 13w3d — IQ at 3 was 99.2 vs 100.0 (Lazarus 2012), and 101.8 vs 102.3 at 9.5 with a third of treated mothers over-replaced (Hales 2018); the MFMU trials randomised 677 women with subclinical hypothyroidism at 16.7 weeks and 526 with hypothyroxinemia at 17.8 — IQ at 5 was 97 vs 94 and 94 vs 91, neither significant (Casey 2017). Three ways both can be true, and the practical conclusion: ACOG PB 223 (2020) and the ATA 2026 guideline (Korevaar et al.) — test women with a reason, not everyone; repeat mild abnormalities before treating; treatment started after the first trimester hasn't been shown to help. Iodine: severe deficiency costs 12.45 IQ points and maternal iodine in pregnancy recovers 8.7 (Qian 2005, 37 studies, 12,291 children); mild deficiency in 1,040 ALSPAC mothers (median 110 µg/g) went with OR 1.58 for bottom-quartile verbal IQ (Bath 2013); 200 µg/day from 10.7 weeks in 832 mildly deficient women changed nothing at 5–6 years (Gowachirapant 2017); Cochrane 2017 finds nothing established for mild deficiency. The targets: 220 µg RDA, ~250 µg total (WHO, ACOG, ATA), a 150 µg potassium iodide line, never a sustained 500+, never kelp; US pregnant median urinary iodine 144 µg/L,…
Today's action: Tonight, three checks, two of them in the kitchen. One: the bottle from Day 33 — find the iodine line. If it reads 150 µg as potassium iodide, done; if there is no iodine line or it's under 150, buy either a prenatal that has it or a separate 150 µg potassium iodide tablet, and not a kelp or seaweed product however natural the front of the bottle says it is. Two: the salt. Pick up the container by the stove and the one on the table; if neither says iodised, buy a box of iodised table salt tomorrow and put it where the cooking actually happens. Three: the call. If your partner takes levothyroxine and the dose hasn't changed since the positive test, she calls the practice or her endocrinologist tomorrow morning, says she's six weeks pregnant and asks about the dose and a blood test. If she doesn't take it but her mother or sister has a thyroid condition, or she has type 1 diabetes or another autoimmune disease, write 'thyroid test — family history' as question nine on the Day 40 sheet, so it's asked with a reason instead of by default.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 42 · Week 6 — Body: the first look
item.description:
What a six-week scan can and can't show, the heartbeat at a hundred and eleven, the measurement that can move your due date, and the risk that falls with every week it's seen.
Week 6 opens on the first day most practices will scan, and on the day Episode Zero promised: the day the due date — and your day number — can move. Your baby is 4–6 mm at Carnegie stage 13 (NHS: a pea with a tail): neural tube sealed at both ends, leg buds appearing under the arm buds, a looped heart starting to divide, and a face in four pieces — lens disc, closed ear pockets, a flat nasal plate and two pairs of jaw arches — that will meet over the next four weeks. What a transvaginal scan shows today: sac, yolk sac and a bright line with a flicker. The number that sounds wrong: in 2,164 pregnancies the mean embryonic heart rate was 111 bpm at days 42–45, 125 at 46–49, 145 at 50–52 and 157 at 53–56 (Stefos 1998) — so 110 is normal today. What slow actually means (Doubilet & Benson 1995 bands; Radiology 2005, 2,937 pregnancies: first-trimester loss 9.1% with a normal rate, 17.4% borderline, 60.6% slow, 77.9% very slow; slow-then-normal 25.4% vs 7.2%). No heartbeat under 7 mm CRL is a repeat scan in 7–14 days, not a diagnosis (Doubilet 2013, NEJM). M-mode, not Doppler, in the first trimester (AIUM 2020). The crown-rump length: accurate to about five days (Robinson & Fleming 1975; ACOG CO 700 ±5–7 days), and the rule — before 9 0/7 weeks, redate if the scan differs from the period date by more than 5 days, once — worked through with examples; NICE's dating scan sits at 11+2–14+1 for a reason. The risk curve after a heartbeat: 9.4% at 6 completed weeks, 4.2% at 7, 1.5% at 8, 0.5% at 9 (Tong 2008); 7.5% overall at 6–10 weeks, rising with age and falling with gestation (Makrydimas 2003) — so a six-week scan locates and counts, and the eight-week scan reassures. Safety: ACOG CO 723; Newnham's 1993 five-scan trial (RR 1.35 for birthweight <10th centile) answered by the same group's 8-year follow-up of 2,714 children in 2004 (no differences); the FDA's standing warning on home Dopplers. Twins: 30.1 per 1,000 US births (CDC 2024); chorionicity is read before 14 weeks (ISUOG, Khalil 2016) — ask 'one placenta or two' before 'identical'. The scan card: LMP and cycle length on the front, three numbers on the back.
Today's action: One index card for the pregnancy file, next to the Day 40 question sheet, which comes to the scan. Front, filled in tonight: her last period date and usual cycle length (Day 40, question one) and the due date you calculated on Day 28. Back, three blank lines for three numbers to ask for in the room: the crown-rump length in millimetres; the heart rate, and which band it's in for the day; and the ultrasound dating in weeks and days, with the question 'does this change the due date, and by how many days?' If it does, cross out the Day 28 due date, write the new one and tonight's new day number under it, and move every dependent date in your calendar. If the scan isn't this week, fill in the front tonight and leave the back for the day. And one rule said out loud: no Doppler at home, this trimester or any other.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

The risk curve after a heartbeat: 9.4% at 6 completed weeks, 4.2% at 7, 1.5% at 8, 0.5% at 9 (Tong 2008); 7.5% overall at 6–10 weeks, rising with age and falling with gestation (Makrydimas 2003) — so a six-week scan locates and counts, and the eight-week scan reassures. Safety: ACOG CO 723; Newnham's 1993 five-scan trial (RR 1.35 for birthweight <10th centile) answered by the same group's 8-year follow-up of 2,714 children in 2004 (no differences); the FDA's standing warning on home Dopplers. Twins: 30.1 per 1,000 US births (CDC 2024); chorionicity is read before 14 weeks (ISUOG, Khalil 2016) — ask 'one placenta or two' before 'identical'. The scan card: LMP and cycle length on the front, three numbers on the back.

Today's action: One index card for the pregnancy file, next to the Day 40 question sheet, which comes to the scan. Front, filled in tonight: her last period date and usual cycle length (Day 40, question one) and the due date you calculated on Day 28. Back, three blank lines for three numbers to ask for in the room: the crown-rump length in millimetres; the heart rate, and which band it's in for the day; and the ultrasound dating in weeks and days, with the question 'does this change the due date, and by how many days?' If it does, cross out the Day 28 due date, write the new one and tonight's new day number under it, and move every dependent date in your calendar. If the scan isn't this week, fill in the front tonight and leave the back for the day. And one rule said out loud: no Doppler at home, this trimester or any other.

item.title: Day 41 · Week 5 — Myths: bad sickness means a girl, sickness means a healthy pregnancy, and nothing can be done about it
item.description:
The second Myths episode, on the last day of Week 5. Your baby is 3–6 mm at the turn to Carnegie stage 13: the neural tube now closed at both ends, arm paddles, leg buds appearing, the heart starting to divide. Myth one, 'she's that sick, it's a girl' — half right: hyperemesis admissions carry higher odds of a girl (Schiff 2004, 2,110 admissions, OR 1.5; Veenendaal 2011 meta-analysis OR 1.27; Askling 1999), and in 91,666 Japanese pregnancies (Mitsuda 2019) the women with severe sickness had girls 54.1% of the time against 45.2% in the women with none and 48.7% overall — a real population effect and a useless test, five points off a coin. Myth two, 'sickness means a healthy pregnancy' — true on average and false as a sign: in 797 women with every loss counted from the hormone test, nausea halved the hazard of loss and vomiting quartered it (Hinkle 2016, JAMA Intern Med; Koren 2014 review), but a fifth of women with normal live births had no symptoms at all (Gadsby 1993; Lacroix 2000; 17% in JECS), the sickness stops in everyone and stops unevenly (mean cessation Day 84; half relieved by 14 weeks), and at the severe end the association flips to lower birth weight (OR 1.42), SGA (1.28) and preterm birth (1.32); the real signals are the physical ones from Days 28 and 38. Myth three, 'nothing can be done', in three forms: 'it's in her head' (Fairweather 1968 versus Fejzo 2024 in Nature — GDF15 from the feto-placental unit acting on her brainstem, β-thalassaemia women barely sick); 'ride it out' (Cochrane 2015's 'no high-quality evidence' is not 'ineffective'; ACOG PB 189 and RCOG GTG 69 make B6 ± doxylamine first-line and say early treatment may prevent hospital; ginger for nausea in 12 RCTs; thiamine before glucose, with 82 published cases of Wernicke's after a mean 6.6 weeks of vomiting); and 'the medicines are dangerous' (Bendectin, 33 million pregnancies, RR 0.95 for malformations across 27 studies, withdrawn in 1983 over lawsuits, after which admissions for vomiting in pregnancy rose 37% and then 50% per 1,000 births with no fall in malformations — Neutel & Johansen 1995). An emerging footnote on prevention via GDF15 desensitisation (Sharma 2025), labelled as such. Three sentences for the father to say, and the first PUQE score.
Today's action: Tonight, three sentences and one score. The sentences are yours to say so she doesn't have to: to 'it must be a girl' — 'slightly more likely, and a coin would do about as well'; to 'at least it means the baby's healthy' — 'on average, it's not a test, and when it's bad it costs her'; to 'nothing can be done' — 'B6 and doxylamine, first-line in both guidelines, and we have the plan'. Then run the PUQE from Day 37 with her for the first time — hours of nausea, vomits, retches, each scored 1–5 — and write the total and the date in the pregnancy file. If it is 7 or more, question five on yesterday's list moves from the first visit to a phone call to the practice tomorrow morning.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 40 · Week 5 — Protocol: the first-visit question list
item.description:
What the hour contains, the seven screens behind it, and the eight questions to bring in writing.
The second Protocol episode, promised on Day 39. Your baby is 3–5 mm at Carnegie stage 12, the caudal neuropore sealing and the limb buds distinct. The first prenatal visit is late by design: the NHS booking appointment at 8–12 weeks takes about an hour, NICE NG201 offers it by 10+0 weeks and plans 10 visits for a first pregnancy and 7 after that, the US schedule runs monthly to 28 weeks and lands at 12–14 visits, and WHO's 2016 minimum is 8 contacts. What the count buys: Cochrane 2015 (7 trials, >60,000 women) found 14% higher perinatal mortality with reduced visits, entirely from low-income trials with under five visits; in high-income settings neither fewer visits nor hybrid video schedules changed outcomes (Balk 2022), which is why ACOG's 2025 Clinical Consensus 8 now tailors the schedule and accepts telehealth. The hour itself: the history including both parents' family history, three measurements, and the seven screens with their numbers — Rh typing (USPSTF A; the father's blood type matters if she is Rh-negative), full blood count, urine culture (2–10% bacteriuria; treatment cuts pyelonephritis 76%), hepatitis B (A; 3.8% transmission untreated, under 1% with birth prophylaxis), HIV (A; 9–67% untreated vs under 1–3% on treatment), syphilis (A, 2025; 3,882 congenital cases in 2023 vs 334 in 2012, ~90% preventable), rubella, hepatitis C, haemoglobinopathies and STI cultures — then the four NICE risk assessments, including the pre-eclampsia checklist that decides whether aspirin 81 mg starts at 12 weeks (RR 0.85; baseline 4%, high risk ≥8%), the mental-health questions and the domestic-abuse question asked with the partner out of the room. Why to write it down: 40–80% of medical information is forgotten immediately and half of the rest is wrong (Kessels 2003); question lists before consultations raise question-asking and satisfaction in 33 RCTs of 8,244 patients (Kinnersley, Cochrane 2007). Then the eight questions, in the order the visit runs, each anchored to Days 28–39: dating, the scan, the screening menu including carrier screening and the father's family history, the medication and supplement audit, the nausea plan, the risk flags (aspirin, Rh), logistics and travel, and screening for both parents. And how to run the room: who writes, recording, teach-back, the notes, and whose appointment it is.
Today's action: Tonight, write the eight questions on one sheet in your own handwriting, with space under each for the answer, and put it in the pregnancy file: (1) our due date from her LMP and cycle length, and will the scan change it; (2) when is the first scan, what for, transvaginal?; (3) which bloods today and how we get results, plus which chromosomal screening is offered and when, and whether carrier screening should be done now; (4) the medication and supplement audit — bring the bottles and the label photo; (5) the nausea plan — B6, dose, doxylamine, call thresholds; (6) the risk flags — aspirin from 12 weeks, Rh status and whether my blood type matters; (7) how many visits, which by video, the after-hours number, and the booked trip; (8) will both of us be screened for depression. On the back, write your own family history and ancestry and ask your parents tomorrow about anything you're unsure of; then find out your blood type.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 39 · Week 5 — Adventure: heat and hydration
item.description:
The one line that matters, what seventy studies found, and how to run a hot trip with a five-week embryo.
The second Adventure episode: the summer trip, the festival, the hot hike. Your baby is 3–5 mm at the turn to Carnegie stage 12, the neural tube sealing at both ends this week and the arm buds appearing; today is also the mean day of onset of pregnancy sickness. Her thermostat: core temperature is highest in the first trimester (37.1 °C at 8 weeks) and falls through pregnancy, with the neutral room temperature dropping 4 °C by 36 weeks (Hartgill 2011); a hot exposure raises maternal core temperature by 0.5 °C, maternal heart rate by 38 bpm and fetal heart rate by 13 bpm on pooled data from 201,906 women (Bonell 2026). The line: 39.0 °C is the teratogenic threshold behind the Day 36 neural-tube evidence, and in 12 studies of 347 pregnant women under exercise and heat no one reached it — land exercise averaged 38.3 °C, max 38.9 (Ravanelli 2019), whose limits (35 min at 80–90% HRmax at 25 °C; water ≤33.4 °C for 45 min; 40 °C bath or 70 °C sauna for 20 min) keep her under it; the CDC's heat-stroke line, 103 °F, is the same temperature from her side. The weather: heatwaves raise preterm birth odds 16% and stillbirth 5% per °C, mostly in late pregnancy, with 'relatively small' summary effects (Chersich 2020, 70 studies); in the first trimester, 10+ days ≥30 °C in weeks 2–8 post-conception add about one heart defect per 1,000 births, concentrated in atrial septal defects (Auger 2017, 704,209 fetuses); miscarriage odds ratios of 1.1–1.2 with intervals touching one (Wesselink 2024; Xu 2025; Das 2023). Water: 2.3 L/day total (EFSA) to 3.0 L (IOM), 70–80% from drinks; the urine colour chart validated in pregnancy — 1–3 fine, ≥4 drink (McKenzie & Armstrong 2017). The field manual: timing, exertion, water, the CDC fan rule (not above 90 °F), cool rooms, the two symptom sets (heat exhaustion vs heat stroke) and the first-trimester trap of mistaking heat illness for pregnancy symptoms.
Today's action: Tonight, ten minutes. Fill a one-litre insulated bottle, put it where her keys live, and agree the rule: it goes everywhere she goes and comes home empty twice a day. Save a picture of the urine colour chart to both phones next to the PUQE score from Day 37 — four means drink. Then open the heat forecast for the next trip or hot weekend: if it is in the top categories, move the hard parts of the day to before ten and after six, keep hard efforts to the cool hours, and find the air conditioning in advance. Hot tubs and saunas stay off the list until Day 42; the pool is the answer.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.

item.title: Day 38 · Week 5 — Parents: sex, sleep and stress in the first trimester
item.description:
What the cohorts actually find, and the one variable that moves the outcomes.
The second Parents episode. Your baby is 2.5–4.5 mm at Carnegie stage 11, the rostral neuropore closing and the heart looped and beating. Sex: half of women worry it will harm the pregnancy and only 29% ever discuss it with a clinician (Bartellas 2000); the NHS position is that it is safe unless told otherwise, with the exceptions specific and mostly later; 59 studies find no harm without risk factors (von Sydow 1999); in a UK case-control study of 6,719 women, feeling well enough for sex went with less miscarriage, not more (Maconochie 2007), and the same reverse-causation pattern holds for preterm birth (Sayle 2001). Bleeding: 27% of 4,510 women bled in the first trimester; spotting carried no measurable excess risk (OR 1.1), heavy bleeding with pain tripled it (Hasan 2009) — so every episode gets a call and almost none is bad news. Desire goes up in some women and down in most; what couples lack is the conversation. Sleep: 76% poor quality, 38% insufficient, 100% waking, 78% napping, in every month of pregnancy (Mindell 2015, 2,427 women) — the split starts now. The relationship: the measured decline is after the birth and pre-pregnancy satisfaction and planning protect against it (Lawrence 2008, 156 couples); emotional intimacy and conflict management move satisfaction more than sex does (Ramsdell 2020, 154 couples); first-time fathers already cut their drinking most (MoBa, 82,362 couples). Stress, read honestly: miscarriage OR 1.42 in a meta-analysis of eight mostly retrospective studies; the bereavement registers (3 million and 4.9 million births) as the ceiling — stillbirth +18%, preterm +7%; anxiety symptoms with no association to perinatal outcomes across 50 studies; child cognition r = −0.05. The buffer in every study is the relationship.
Today's action: Tonight, one conversation, fifteen minutes, three questions you ask: (1) about sex this trimester — what do you want, and what should I stop guessing about? — and take the answer as the week's rule; (2) what time do you want to be asleep by this week? — set it as the household bedtime and end the evening there; (3) what is the one thing on your list I could just take? — take it by the weekend. If there has been any bleeding, the fourth question is for the practice in the morning, not for her.
The Empirical Dad is a personal research briefing, not medical advice. Decisions about pregnancy, birth and infant care belong with your OB, midwife and pediatrician.
